cards.why: Vulnerability scanners detect misconfigurations such as a disabled host firewall and default administrator credentials on network devices.

whyNot.B: SSH on servers is often legitimate and enabled by design, so it is not inherently a misconfiguration.
whyNot.C: Browser homepages are a cosmetic setting, not a security misconfiguration.
whyNot.E: Checking for updates daily is an acceptable configuration and not a vulnerability.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing patches on servers. One of the servers is reporting the following error message in the WSUS management console: The computer has not reported status in 30 days. Given this scenario, which of the following statements BEST represents the issue with the output above?
A. The computer in question has not pulled the latest ACL policies for the firewall.
B. The computer in question has not pulled the latest GPO policies from the management server.
C. The computer in question has not pulled the latest antivirus definitions from the antivirus program.
D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.back: D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.why: WSUS manages Windows and Microsoft software updates, so a computer not reporting status for 30 days has not pulled the latest updates and patches.

whyNot.A: Firewall ACL policies are not distributed or tracked through WSUS.
whyNot.B: GPO policies come from Active Directory and are not reported in the WSUS console.
whyNot.C: Antivirus definitions are delivered by the antivirus management system, not WSUS status reporting.

cards.front:
Two users must encrypt and transmit large amount of data between them. Which of the following should they use to encrypt and transmit the data?
A. Symmetric algorithm
B. Hash function
C. Digital signature
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: Symmetric algorithms such as AES are fast and efficient, making them the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two parties.

whyNot.B: A hash function produces a fixed digest and is one-way, so it cannot encrypt data for later decryption.
whyNot.C: A digital signature provides authentication and integrity, not bulk data encryption.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning without real cryptographic protection and is not suitable for secure transmission.

cards.front:
A security administrator is reviewing the following PowerShell script referenced in the Task Scheduler on a database server: $members = GetADGroupMemeber -Identity "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Select - ExpandProperty name if ($members -notcontains "JohnDoe"){ Remove-Item -path C:\Database -recurse -force } Which of the following did the security administrator discover?
A. Ransomeware
B. Backdoor
C. Logic bomb
D. Trojan
cards.why: The script deletes the database folder if JohnDoe is not in Domain Admins, a malicious action triggered by a condition, which defines a logic bomb.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, whereas this script simply deletes files.
whyNot.B: A backdoor provides covert remote access, and nothing in the script does that.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software, while this is a conditionally triggered script.

cards.front:
A bank is experiencing a DoS attack against an application designed to handle 500IP-based sessions. in addition, the perimeter router can only handle 1Gbps of traffic. Which of the following should be implemented to prevent a DoS attacks in the future?
A. Deploy multiple web servers and implement a load balancer
B. Increase the capacity of the perimeter router to 10 Gbps
C. Install a firewall at the network to prevent all attacks
D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.back: D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.why: Redundancy across network devices and services removes single points of failure, such as the limited router and session capacity, improving resilience against DoS attacks.

whyNot.A: Load balancing web servers helps the application but leaves the 1Gbps router as a bottleneck.
whyNot.B: Upgrading the router addresses bandwidth only and leaves the session limit and other single points of failure.
whyNot.C: No firewall can prevent all attacks, and a single firewall can itself be overwhelmed.

cards.keyDoubt: A. Multiple servers behind a load balancer directly address the 500-session limit, which is the most concrete and common answer for this scenario.

cards.front:
A malicious system continuously sends an extremely large number of SYN packets to a server. Which of the following BEST describes the resulting effect?
A. The server will be unable to server clients due to lack of bandwidth
B. the server's firewall will be unable to effectively filter traffic due to the amount of data transmitted
C. The server will crash when trying to reassemble all the fragmented packets
D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.back: D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.why: A SYN flood leaves many half-open connections in the server's connection table, consuming memory and resources until legitimate clients cannot connect.

whyNot.A: SYN floods exhaust connection resources and do not necessarily saturate bandwidth.
whyNot.B: A SYN flood targets the server's connection state, not the firewall's filtering capacity.
whyNot.C: Reassembling fragmented packets relates to fragmentation attacks, not SYN floods.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is deploying a new mission essential server into a virtual environment. Which of the following is BEST mitigated by the environment's rapid elasticity characteristic?
A. Data confidentiality breaches
B. VM escape attacks
C. Lack of redundancy
D. Denial of service
cards.why: Rapid elasticity lets the environment automatically scale resources up under a traffic flood, absorbing the load and mitigating denial of service impact on availability.

whyNot.A: Elasticity adds capacity and does nothing to protect data confidentiality.
whyNot.B: VM escape is a hypervisor vulnerability, not something extra capacity prevents.
whyNot.C: Redundancy comes from failover and clustering, not from elastic scaling of capacity.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the proper order for logging a user into a system from the first step to the last step?
A. Identification, authentication, authorization
B. Identification, authorization, authentication
C. Authentication, identification, authorization
D. Authentication, identification, authorization
E. Authorization, identification, authentication
cards.why: A user first claims an identity (identification), then proves it (authentication), and only then is granted permissions (authorization).

whyNot.B: Authorization cannot occur before the identity has been verified through authentication.
whyNot.C: Authentication needs a claimed identity first, so identification must come before it.
whyNot.D: This repeats the wrong order of C; authentication cannot precede identification.
whyNot.E: Authorization is the last step, since permissions depend on a verified identity.

cards.front:
A company stores highly sensitive data files used by the accounting system on a server file share. The accounting system uses a service account named accounting-svc to access the file share. The data is protected will a full disk encryption, and the permissions are set as follows: File system permissions: Users = Read Only Share permission: accounting-svc = Read Only Given the listed protections are in place and unchanged, to which of the following risks is the data still subject?
A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
B. Theft of physical hard drives and a breach of confidentiality
C. Remote exfiltration of data using domain credentials
D. Disclosure of sensitive data to third parties due to excessive share permissions
cards.back: A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
cards.why: Full disk encryption only protects data at rest while the system is powered off, so someone with local console access to the running, unlocked server could still copy data out.

whyNot.B: Full disk encryption specifically protects against stolen drives, so this risk is mitigated.
whyNot.C: Share permissions allow only accounting-svc, so ordinary domain user credentials cannot read the share remotely.
whyNot.D: The share permission is restricted to a single read-only service account, so it is not excessive.

cards.front:
A bank uses a wireless network to transmit credit card purchases to a billing system. Which of the following would be MOST appropriate to protect credit card information from being accessed by unauthorized individuals outside of the premises?
A. Air gap
B. Infrared detection
C. Faraday cage
D. Protected distributions
cards.why: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals, preventing wireless transmissions from leaking outside the premises where unauthorized people could capture them.

whyNot.A: An air gap removes network connectivity, which is incompatible with a wireless transmission requirement.
whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not contain wireless signals.
whyNot.D: Protected distribution secures physical cabling, not wireless transmissions.

cards.front:
Joe, a salesman, was assigned to a new project that requires him to travel to a client site. While waiting for a flight, Joe decides to connect to the airport wireless network without connecting to a VPN, and then sends confidential emails to fellow colleagues. A few days later, the company experiences a data breach. Upon investigation, the company learns Joe's emails were intercepted. Which of the following MOST likely caused the data breach?
A. Policy violation
B. Social engineering
C. Insider threat
D. Zero--day attack
cards.why: Joe broke the company's acceptable use and remote access policy by sending confidential email over an untrusted public network without a VPN, which exposed the data to interception.

whyNot.B: No one manipulated Joe into acting; he chose to use the public network himself.
whyNot.C: Joe did not act maliciously, so this is carelessness rather than an insider threat.
whyNot.D: Interception over open Wi-Fi uses known techniques, not an unknown vulnerability.

cards.front:
A help desk technician receives a phone call from an individual claiming to be an employee of the organization and requesting assistance to access a locked account. The help desk technician asks the individual to provide proof of identity before access can be granted. Which of the following types of attack is the caller performing?
A. Phishing
B. Shoulder surfing
C. Impersonation
D. Dumpster diving
cards.why: The caller is pretending to be a legitimate employee to gain account access, which is impersonation, a social engineering technique.

whyNot.A: Phishing uses deceptive email or messages, and this attack is a phone call, which would be vishing.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing means watching someone enter sensitive information, which did not happen here.
whyNot.D: Dumpster diving means searching discarded materials, which is not what the caller is doing.

cards.front:
Confidential emails from an organization were posted to a website without the organization's knowledge. Upon investigation, it was determined that the emails were obtained from an internal actor who sniffed the emails in plain text. Which of the following protocols, if properly implemented, would have MOST likely prevented the emails from being sniffed? (Select TWO)
A. Secure IMAP
B. DNSSEC
C. S/MIME
D. SMTPS
E. HTTPS
cards.back:
C. S/MIME
D. SMTPS

SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) is a deprecated method for securing SMTP with transport layer security. It is intended to provide authentication of the communication partners, as well as data integrity and confidentiality.
cards.why: S/MIME encrypts the message content end to end, and SMTPS encrypts mail transport, so emails could not be read in plain text by someone sniffing the network.

whyNot.A: Secure IMAP only protects mailbox retrieval, leaving message content and server-to-server transport exposed.
whyNot.B: DNSSEC authenticates DNS records and does not encrypt email content.
whyNot.E: HTTPS protects web traffic and does not secure email protocols unless webmail is used.

cards.front:
A company wants to implement an access management solution that allows employees to use the same usernames and passwords for multiple applications without having to keep multiple credentials synchronized. Which of the following solutions would BEST meet these requirements?
A. Multifactor authentication
B. SSO
C. Biometrics
D. PKI
E. Federation
cards.why: Single sign-on lets users authenticate once with one set of credentials and access multiple applications without maintaining separate synchronized accounts.

whyNot.A: Multifactor authentication strengthens login but does not unify credentials across applications.
whyNot.C: Biometrics is an authentication factor and does not provide shared access across applications.
whyNot.D: PKI manages certificates and keys and does not provide a single credential for multiple applications.

cards.front:
An external auditor visits the human resources department and performs a physical security assessment. The auditor observed documents on printers that are unclaimed. A closer look at these documents reveals employee names, addresses, ages, and types of medical and dental coverage options each employee has selected. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate actions to take?
A. Flip the documents face down so no one knows these documents are PII sensitive
B. Shred the documents and let the owner print the new set
C. Retrieve the documents, label them with a PII cover sheet, and return them to the printer
D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.back: D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.why: The auditor found a privacy policy violation involving PII and PHI, so the proper action is reporting it to the responsible HR manager for corrective action.

whyNot.A: Flipping documents over leaves the sensitive data unprotected and does not address the violation.
whyNot.B: Shredding destroys records the owner may need and bypasses proper incident handling.
whyNot.C: Handling the documents and returning them to the printer leaves them exposed and is not a proper response.

cards.front:
Which of the following authentication concepts is a gait analysis MOST closely associated?
A. Somewhere you are
B. Something you are
C. Something you do
D. Something you know
cards.why: Gait analysis measures how a person walks, which is a behavioral trait and falls under the something you do authentication factor.

whyNot.A: Somewhere you are relies on location, such as GPS or IP address.
whyNot.B: Something you are covers physical traits like fingerprints, while gait is a behavior.
whyNot.D: Something you know covers secrets such as passwords or PINs.

cards.front:
Which of the following metrics are used to calculate the SLE? (Select TWO)
A. ROI
B. ARO
C. ALE
D. MTBF
E. MTTF
F. TCO
cards.why: SLE can be derived from ALE and ARO, since ALE equals SLE multiplied by ARO, so dividing ALE by ARO yields SLE.

whyNot.A: ROI measures financial return on an investment and is not part of the SLE calculation.
whyNot.D: MTBF measures average time between repairable failures and does not determine loss per incident.
whyNot.E: MTTF measures expected time to failure of non-repairable systems and is not an SLE input.
whyNot.F: TCO is the total cost of owning an asset over its life, not a per-incident loss figure.

cards.front:
Due to regulatory requirements, server in a global organization must use time synchronization. Which of the following represents the MOST secure method of time synchronization?
A. The server should connect to external Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
C. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
D. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
cards.back:
B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization

Configure your own Internal NTP hierarchical service for your network. It is possible to purchase Stratum 1 or Stratum 0 NTP appliances to use internally for less than the cost of a typical server.
cards.why: An internal Stratum 0 time source such as a GPS or atomic clock keeps synchronization inside the organization, avoiding exposure to external attacks or spoofed time.

whyNot.A: Relying on external servers exposes time synchronization to interception and spoofing over untrusted networks.
whyNot.C: External Stratum 1 servers still depend on traffic over untrusted networks that can be manipulated.
whyNot.D: This is identical to C and has the same external trust weakness.

cards.front:
When sending messages using symmetric encryption, which of the following must happen FIRST?
A. Exchange encryption key
B. Establish digital signatures
C. Agree on an encryption method
D. Install digital certificates
cards.back: C. Agree on an encryption method
cards.why: Both parties must first agree on the encryption algorithm and method before they can generate and exchange the shared key that symmetric encryption requires.

whyNot.A: Keys cannot be exchanged until the parties know which encryption method and key type to use.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authentication and integrity and are not required to begin symmetric encryption.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates support asymmetric key distribution and are not a prerequisite for agreeing on symmetric encryption.

cards.front:
Which of the following scenarios BEST describes an implementation of non-repudiation?
A. A user logs into a domain workstation and access network file shares for another department
B. A user remotely logs into the mail server with another user's credentials
C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
D. A user access the workstation registry to make unauthorized changes to enable functionality within an application
cards.back: C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
cards.why: A digitally signed email proves the sender originated the message, so the sender cannot later deny sending it, which is non-repudiation.

whyNot.A: This describes access to resources and does not tie an action irrefutably to a user.
whyNot.B: Using another user's credentials is impersonation, which defeats non-repudiation.
whyNot.D: Unauthorized registry changes are a misuse of privileges and prove nothing about who sent or signed.

cards.front:
An office manager found a folder that included documents with various types of data relating to corporate clients. The office manager notified the data included dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers for the clients. The office manager then reported this finding to the security compliance officer. Which of the following portions of the policy would the security officer need to consult to determine if a breach has occurred?
A. Public
B. Private
C. PHI
D. PII
cards.why: Dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers are personally identifiable information, so the officer would consult the PII portion of the policy to assess whether a breach occurred.

whyNot.A: Public data is intended for open release, which does not describe client personal information.
whyNot.B: Private is a generic classification and does not specifically govern identifying personal data.
whyNot.C: PHI covers health information held by covered entities, and no medical data was found here.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an asymmetric function that generates a new and separate key every time it runs?
A. RSA
B. DSA
C. DHE
D. HMAC
E. PBKDF2
cards.back:
C. DHE

Although Diffie-Hellman key agreement itself is a non-authenticated key-agreement protocol, it provides the basis for a variety of authenticated protocols, and is used to provide forward secrecy in Transport Layer Security's ephemeral modes (referred to as EDH...
cards.why: DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) generates a new, separate key pair for every session, providing perfect forward secrecy using an asymmetric key exchange.

whyNot.A: RSA uses a long-lived key pair and does not generate a new key on each run.
whyNot.B: DSA is a signature algorithm using a static key pair, not a per-run key generator.
whyNot.D: HMAC is a symmetric keyed hash, not an asymmetric function.
whyNot.E: PBKDF2 is a key stretching function that derives keys from passwords, and it is not asymmetric.

cards.front:
Which of the following would be considered multifactor authentication?
A. Hardware token and smart card
B. Voice recognition and retina scan
C. Strong password and fingerprint
D. PIN and security questions
cards.why: A strong password (something you know) combined with a fingerprint (something you are) uses two different authentication factor categories, which is true multifactor authentication.

whyNot.A: A hardware token and a smart card are both something you have, so only one factor type.
whyNot.B: Voice recognition and a retina scan are both biometrics (something you are), so only one factor type.
whyNot.D: A PIN and security questions are both something you know, so only one factor type.

cards.front:
Users report the following message appear when browsing to the company's secure site: This website cannot be trusted. Which of the following actions should a security analyst take to resolve these messages? (Select TWO)
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server
B. Ensure the certificate has a .pfx extension on the server
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store
D. Install the updated private key on the web server
E. Have users clear their browsing history and relaunch the session
cards.back:
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store
cards.why: An untrusted site warning usually means the server certificate has expired or the client does not trust the issuing CA, so verifying expiration and updating the root certificate in the client store resolves it.

whyNot.B: A .pfx file extension only describes the file format and does not affect whether clients trust the certificate.
whyNot.D: The private key stays on the server and is not what clients validate, so replacing it does not fix trust errors.
whyNot.E: Clearing browsing history does not change certificate validation or trust.

cards.front:
Despite having implemented password policies, users continue to set the same weak passwords and reuse old passwords. Which of the following technical controls would help prevent these policy violations?
A. Password expiration
B. Password length
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
E. Password lockout
cards.back:
A. Password expiration
D. Password history
cards.why: Password history blocks reuse of old passwords, and expiration forces periodic changes so users cannot keep the same password indefinitely.

whyNot.B: Password length sets a minimum size but does not stop users from reusing old passwords.
whyNot.C: Password complexity enforces character types but does not prevent reuse of previous passwords.
whyNot.E: Password lockout limits failed login attempts and does not control password choice or reuse.

cards.keyDoubt: C. The question mentions weak passwords, which complexity addresses, and history addresses reuse, so D and C fit better than expiration, which can encourage weaker passwords.

cards.front:
A security auditor is testing perimeter security in a building that is protected by badge readers. Which of the following types of attacks would MOST likely gain access?
A. Phishing
B. Man-in-the-middle
C. Tailgating
D. Watering hole
E. Shoulder surfing
cards.why: Tailgating means following an authorized person through a badge-controlled door, which bypasses the badge reader and is the most likely way a perimeter tester gains physical access.

whyNot.A: Phishing is a deceptive message attack and does not defeat a physical badge reader.
whyNot.B: Man-in-the-middle intercepts network communications and is not a physical entry technique.
whyNot.D: A watering hole attack compromises websites that targets visit and is not physical.
whyNot.E: Shoulder surfing observes someone entering credentials, which does not help against a badge reader.

cards.front:
Which of the following encryption methods does PKI typically use to securely protect keys?
A. Elliptic curve
B. Digital signatures
C. Asymmetric
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: PKI relies on asymmetric cryptography, where public and private key pairs are used to protect keys and establish trust through certificates.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is a specific asymmetric algorithm family and not the general method PKI uses.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authenticity and integrity and are not an encryption method.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides data without real cryptographic protection and is not used by PKI.

cards.front:
A department head at a university resigned on the first day of spring semester. It was subsequently determined that the department head deleted numerous files and directories from the server-based home directory while the campus was closed. Which of the following policies or procedures could have prevented this form occurring?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Permissions auditing and review
C. Offboarding
D. Account expiration
cards.why: Offboarding procedures disable or remove access when an employee resigns, which would have prevented the department head from deleting files after leaving.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit login hours but would not stop access during normal permitted times.
whyNot.B: Permissions auditing finds excess rights but would not revoke access of a departing employee.
whyNot.D: Account expiration applies to accounts with preset end dates, and the departure date here was not known in advance.

cards.front:
An organization wants to upgrade its enterprise-wide desktop computer solution. The organization currently has 500 PCs active on the network. the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) suggests that the organization employ desktop imaging technology for such a large scale upgrade. Which of the following is a security benefit of implementing an imaging solution?
A. it allows for faster deployment
B. it provides a consistent baseline
C. It reduces the number of vulnerabilities
D. It decreases the boot time
cards.back: B. it provides a consistent baseline
cards.why: Imaging deploys the same hardened configuration to every PC, creating a consistent security baseline that makes systems predictable and easier to audit.

whyNot.A: Faster deployment is an operational benefit rather than a security benefit.
whyNot.C: Imaging does not reduce vulnerabilities by itself, since the image can contain unpatched software.
whyNot.D: Boot time is a performance matter and has no security value.

cards.front:
A senior incident response manager receives a call about some external IPs communicating with internal computers during off hours. Which of the following types of malware is MOST likely causing this issue?
A. Botnet
B. Ransomware
C. Polymorphic malware
D. Armored virus
cards.why: A botnet consists of compromised hosts that communicate with external command and control servers, often during off hours, matching the unexpected external IP traffic.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and does not primarily show as ongoing external communication.
whyNot.C: Polymorphic malware changes its code to evade detection, which does not explain the external communication.
whyNot.D: An armored virus resists analysis by obfuscating its code, which does not explain the external communication.

cards.front:
An organization has implemented an IPSec VPN access for remote users. Which of the following IPSec modes would be the MOST secure for this organization to implement?
A. Tunnel mode
B. Transport mode
C. AH-only mode
D. ESP-only mode
cards.back:
A. Tunnel mode

In both ESP and AH cases with IPSec Transport mode, the IP header is exposed. The IP header is not exposed in IPSec Tunnel mode.
cards.why: Tunnel mode encrypts and encapsulates the entire original packet including the header, which is most secure and standard for remote access VPNs.

whyNot.B: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves original IP headers exposed.
whyNot.C: AH provides integrity and authentication but no encryption, so it is less secure.
whyNot.D: ESP-only is an option within a mode and does not specify the more secure header-protecting encapsulation.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a wireless network with EAP-TLS. Which of the following activities is a requirement for this configuration?
A. Setting up a TACACS+ server
B. Configuring federation between authentication servers
C. Enabling TOTP
D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.back: D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.why: EAP-TLS uses mutual certificate authentication, so client devices must be issued digital certificates in addition to the server certificate.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ is a device administration AAA protocol and is not required for EAP-TLS.
whyNot.B: Federation links identity providers and is not required for EAP-TLS wireless authentication.
whyNot.C: TOTP is a one-time password method and is not used by EAP-TLS.

cards.front:
Several workstations on a network are found to be on OS versions that are vulnerable to a specific attack. Which of the following is considered to be a corrective action to combat this vulnerability?
A. Install an antivirus definition patch
B. Educate the workstation users
C. Leverage server isolation
D. Install a vendor-supplied patch
E. Install an intrusion detection system
cards.why: Installing the vendor-supplied patch fixes the underlying OS vulnerability, which is a corrective control that removes the weakness.

whyNot.A: Antivirus definitions detect known malware and do not patch an OS vulnerability.
whyNot.B: User education is an administrative control and does not fix the vulnerable OS.
whyNot.C: Server isolation limits exposure but does not correct the vulnerability on workstations.
whyNot.E: An IDS only detects attacks and is a detective control, so it does not correct the vulnerability.

cards.front:
A user suspects someone has been accessing a home network without permission by spoofing the MAC address of an authorized system. While attempting to determine if an unauthorized user is logging into the home network, the user reviews the wireless router, which shows the following table for systems that are currently on the home network: Hostname IP Address MAC MAC Filter DadPC 192.168.1.15 00:1D:1A:44:17:B5 On MomPC 192.168.1.15 21:13:D6:C5:42:A2 Off JuniorPC 192.168.2.16 42:A7:D1:25:11:52 On Unknown 192.168.1.18 10:B3:22:1A:FF:21 Off Which of the following should be the NEXT step to determine if there is an unauthorized user on the network?
A. Apply MAC filtering and see if the router drops any of the systems
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network
C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host
D. Conduct a ping sweep of each of the authorized systems and see if an echo response is received
cards.back:
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network

Dad's PC and Mom's PC have the same IP address. One of them is doing ARP spoofing.
cards.why: Physically checking each authorized system confirms whether it is actually online, so any entry that does not match a real device indicates a spoofed MAC or an intruder.

whyNot.A: Applying MAC filtering is easily bypassed by spoofing and does not identify who is actually connected.
whyNot.C: Denying the unknown host only blocks one device and does not determine if MAC spoofing is occurring.
whyNot.D: A ping sweep may be blocked and cannot distinguish a real device from a spoofed address.

cards.front:
The POODLE attack is an MITM exploit that affects:
A. TLS1.0 with CBC mode cipher
B. SSLv2.0 with CBC mode cipher
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher
D. SSLv3.0 with ECB mode cipher
cards.back:
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher

A flaw was found in the way SSL 3.0 handled padding bytes when decrypting messages encrypted using block ciphers in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode.
cards.why: POODLE exploits SSLv3.0 CBC mode padding handling, letting a man-in-the-middle decrypt bytes of encrypted traffic through a protocol downgrade.

whyNot.A: The original POODLE targets SSLv3, though some TLS 1.0 implementations had a related padding flaw.
whyNot.B: SSLv2.0 has other serious flaws and is not the POODLE target.
whyNot.D: ECB mode is not what POODLE exploits, which depends on CBC padding.

cards.front:
Security administrators attempted corrective action after a phishing attack. Users are still experiencing trouble logging in, as well as an increase in account lockouts. Users' email contacts are complaining of an increase in spam and social networking requests. Due to the large number of affected accounts, remediation must be accomplished quickly. Which of the following actions should be taken FIRST? (Select TWO)
A. Disable the compromised accounts
B. Update WAF rules to block social networks
C. Remove the compromised accounts with all AD groups
D. Change the compromised accounts' passwords
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework
cards.back:
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is a simple email-validation system designed to detect email spoofing by providing a mechanism to allow receiving mail exchangers to check that incoming mail from a domain comes from a host authorized by that domain's administrato...
cards.why: Disabling the open relay and enabling SPF stops the email server from sending spam and spoofed mail, which quickly contains the spread across many accounts.

whyNot.A: Disabling accounts is slow for a large number of affected accounts and does not stop relay abuse.
whyNot.B: Blocking social networks in the WAF does not address compromised email accounts or spam.
whyNot.C: Removing accounts from AD groups is disruptive and does not stop the spam.
whyNot.D: Changing passwords is necessary but handles accounts individually and is slower with many affected users.

cards.keyDoubt: D. Changing the compromised accounts' passwords directly stops attackers using the accounts, and users report login trouble and lockouts, so the key's relay and SPF answers are questionable.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, wants to ensure credentials are encrypted in transit when implementing a RADIUS server for SSO. Which of the following are needed given these requirements? (Select TWO)
A. Public key
B. Shared key
C. Elliptic curve
D. MD5
E. Private key
F. DES
cards.back:
A. Public key
E. Private key
cards.why: Encrypting credentials in transit relies on asymmetric cryptography: the public key encrypts or verifies and the private key decrypts or signs, as in certificate-based EAP tunnels.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and only protects the RADIUS client-server secret, not the credential exchange with the user.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is an algorithm family, not a key component that must be provisioned.
whyNot.D: MD5 is a weak hashing algorithm and does not encrypt data in transit.
whyNot.F: DES is an obsolete symmetric cipher with a short key and is not appropriate here.

cards.front:
Which of the following allows an auditor to test proprietary-software compiled code for security flaws?
A. Fuzzing
B. Static review
C. Code signing
D. Regression testing
cards.why: Fuzzing sends malformed or random input to running compiled code to expose crashes and flaws, so no source code is required.

whyNot.B: Static review examines source code, which an auditor lacks for proprietary compiled software.
whyNot.C: Code signing verifies publisher and integrity, not the presence of security flaws.
whyNot.D: Regression testing confirms that existing functionality still works after changes, not that the code is free of flaws.

cards.front:
Which of the following s the BEST reason to run an untested application is a sandbox?
A. To allow the application to take full advantage of the host system's resources and storage
B. To utilize the host systems antivirus and firewall applications instead of running it own protection
C. To prevent the application from acquiring escalated privileges and accessing its host system
D. To increase application processing speed so the host system can perform real-time logging
cards.back: C. To prevent the application from acquiring escalated privileges and accessing its host system
cards.why: A sandbox isolates the application so untested code cannot escalate privileges or reach the host system, containing any malicious behavior.

whyNot.A: Sandboxes deliberately restrict access to host resources and storage rather than granting full access.
whyNot.B: Sandboxed code is isolated, and relying on the host's protections instead of its own is not the purpose.
whyNot.D: Sandboxing adds overhead and does not speed up processing or logging.

cards.front:
A manager wants to distribute a report to several other managers within the company. Some of them reside in remote locations that are not connected to the domain but have a local server. Because there is sensitive data within the report and the size is beyond the limit of the email attachment size, emailing the report is not an option. Which of the following protocols should be implemented to distribute the report securely? (Select THREE)
A. S/MIME
B. SSH
C. SNMPv3
D. FTPS
E. SRTP
F. HTTPS
G. LDAPS
cards.back:
B. SSH
D. FTPS
F. HTTPS
cards.why: SSH (SFTP/SCP), FTPS, and HTTPS each provide encrypted transfer of large files to remote servers without email.

whyNot.A: S/MIME secures email messages, and email is ruled out by the size limit.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 is for secure network device management, not file distribution.
whyNot.E: SRTP secures real-time voice and video media streams, not file transfer.
whyNot.G: LDAPS secures directory queries and is not a file distribution protocol.

cards.front:
A company is performing an analysis of the corporate enterprise network with the intent of identifying what will cause losses in revenue, referrals, and/or reputation when out of commission. Which of the following is an element of a BIA that is being addressed?
A. Mission-essential function
B. Single point of failure
C. backup and restoration plans
D. Identification of critical systems
cards.back:
D. Identification of critical systems

The BIA is composed of the following three steps: Determine mission/business processes and recovery criticality.
cards.why: Identifying critical systems is the BIA element that determines which systems cause losses in revenue, referrals, or reputation when unavailable.

whyNot.A: Mission-essential functions are the business processes themselves, whereas the scenario analyzes the systems whose outage causes loss.
whyNot.B: A single point of failure is a resilience weakness, not the BIA element of impact from a system being down.
whyNot.C: Backup and restoration plans are recovery measures that come after the BIA identifies what matters.

cards.front:
Ann, a user, states that her machine has been behaving erratically over the past week. She has experienced slowness and input lag and found text files that appear to contain pieces of her emails or online conversations with coworkers. The technician runs a standard virus scan but detects nothing. Which of the following types of malware has infected the machine?
A. Ransomware
B. Rootkit
C. Backdoor
D. Keylogger
cards.why: A keylogger records keystrokes into text files, causing input lag and capturing emails and chats, and it can evade a standard virus scan.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it would not leave text snippets of conversations.
whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malware presence but does not by itself capture and store typed content.
whyNot.C: A backdoor provides remote access and does not by itself record keystrokes into files.

cards.front:
A security analyst is attempting to identify vulnerabilities in a customer's web application without impacting the system or its data. Which of the following BEST describes the vulnerability scanning concept performed?
A. Aggressive scan
B. Passive scan
C. Non-credentialed scan
D. Compliance scan
cards.back:
B. Passive scan

Passive scanning is a method of vulnerability detection that relies on information gleaned from network data that is captured from a target computer without direct interaction.
cards.why: A passive scan observes traffic or configurations without sending probes, so it identifies vulnerabilities without impacting the system or its data.

whyNot.A: Aggressive scans actively probe and can disrupt services or alter data.
whyNot.C: Non-credentialed scans describe access level and still send active probes that may affect the system.
whyNot.D: A compliance scan checks against a policy baseline and does not describe the non-impact approach.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to implement a wireless protocol that will allow the organization to authenticate mobile devices prior to providing the user with a captive portal login. Which of the following should the systems administrator configure?
A. L2TP with MAC filtering
B. EAP-TTLS
C. WPA2-CCMP with PSK
D. RADIUS federation
cards.back:
D. RADIUS federation

RADIUS generally includes 802.1X that pre-authenticates devices.
cards.why: RADIUS federation authenticates devices or users at the network edge through 802.1X before any captive portal login is presented.

whyNot.A: L2TP is a tunneling protocol and MAC filtering is easily spoofed, so neither provides proper pre-portal authentication.
whyNot.B: EAP-TTLS is an authentication method that needs a RADIUS backend and does not provide the federated device authentication described.
whyNot.C: WPA2-CCMP with PSK uses one shared passphrase and does not authenticate individual devices.

cards.front:
A user receives an email from ISP indicating malicious traffic coming from the user's home network is detected. The traffic appears to be Linux-based, and it is targeting a website that was recently featured on the news as being taken offline by an Internet attack. The only Linux device on the network is a home surveillance camera system. Which of the following BEST describes what is happening?
A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
B. The camera system is infected with a RAT.
C. The camera system is infected with a Trojan.
D. The camera system is infected with a backdoor.
cards.back: A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
cards.why: A compromised IoT camera taking part in an attack on a third-party site is a bot in a botnet, used for DDoS.

whyNot.B: A RAT gives an attacker interactive remote control, but the scenario describes attack traffic against another site.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, which describes the delivery method, not the participation in the attack.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is just a hidden access path and does not explain the coordinated attack traffic.

cards.front:
While on a business trip, a user's mobile device goes missing. The user immediately contacts the organization's service desk to report the incident. Which of the following actions is the best response to protect the data stored on the user's mobile device.
A. Encrypt all of the data on the device
B. Remotely wipe the mobile device via the mobile device manager to ensure the data is not compromised.
C. Report the device as lost or stolen to the authorities
D. Call the help desk to change your password
cards.back: B. Remotely wipe the mobile device via the mobile device manager to ensure the data is not compromised.
cards.why: Remote wipe through the mobile device manager erases the data immediately, protecting it even though the device is out of the owner's hands.

whyNot.A: Encrypting data requires access to the device, which is already missing.
whyNot.C: Reporting to authorities may help recovery but does not protect the data on the device.
whyNot.D: Changing a password does not remove data stored locally on the device.

cards.front:
A security analyst launches the Task Manager on a server with poor performance, and notices private bytes are being exhausted and the application pool is constantly recycling. Which of the following Best describes the cause of the negative impact to application availability?
A. Integer Overflow
B. Buffer Overflow
C. Race Condition
D. Memory Leaks
cards.back:
D. Memory Leaks

Private Bytes refer to the amount of memory that the process executable has asked for - not necessarily the amount it is actually using. They are "private" because they (usually) exclude memory-mapped files (i.e. shared DLLs).
cards.why: A memory leak steadily consumes private bytes until the pool is exhausted, forcing the application pool to recycle and hurting availability.

whyNot.A: An integer overflow produces wrong values or crashes at a specific operation, not steady memory exhaustion.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow overwrites adjacent memory and does not gradually consume private bytes.
whyNot.C: A race condition arises from timing between threads and does not cause progressive memory consumption.

cards.front:
While trying to manage a firewall's ACL, a security administrator (User3) receives an "Access Denied" error. The manager reviews the following information. Security_admins: User1, User2 Firewall Access ACL Read: Security_admins ACL Write: Security_admins Reboot: Managers Audit: User3 Which of the following is preventing the administrator from
A. Rule based access control
B. Mandatory access control
C. Discretionary access's control
D. RBAC
cards.why: Rule-based access control enforces predefined rules in the ACL, and the rules grant User3 only Audit, so the write request is denied.

whyNot.B: Mandatory access control relies on classification labels and clearances, which are not shown here.
whyNot.C: Discretionary access control lets resource owners grant access at their discretion, which is not what is shown.
whyNot.D: RBAC assigns permissions by job role, but the denial here comes from the explicit ACL rules.

cards.front:
Which of the following are the differences between incremental and differential backups?
A. Both backup types or almost identical except for the time that the backup is run
B. Differential backup take less time to complete
C. Incremental backups take less time than differential
D. Incremental backup back up all of the data since the last differential
E. Differential backups take more time to restore than incremental backups
F. Differential backups only backup files since the last full backup
cards.back:
C. Incremental backups take less time than differential
F. Differential backups only backup files since the last full backup
cards.why: Incremental backups copy only changes since the last backup, so they run faster, while differential backups copy everything changed since the last full backup.

whyNot.A: The two types differ in what they copy, not just when they run.
whyNot.B: Differentials grow larger each day and take longer to back up than incrementals.
whyNot.D: Incrementals back up data since the last backup of any type, not since the last differential.
whyNot.E: Differentials restore faster because only the full backup plus the latest differential are needed.

cards.front:
A security analyst has been dealing with a large number of malware infections on workstations with legacy operating systems. The infections are not being detected by the current AV suite. Further analysis shows that the signatures are up to date and the AV engines are functioning correctly. The company is unable to afford next-generation AV that prevents these attacks. Which of the following methods should the security analyst employ to prevent future outbreaks?
A. Application Blacklisting
B. Application Whitelisting
C. Blockchain analysis
D. Strong ACL's
cards.why: Application whitelisting allows only approved programs to run, which blocks unknown malware on legacy systems even when AV signatures miss it.

whyNot.A: Blacklisting blocks only known-bad applications, which is the same limitation that lets the malware slip past AV.
whyNot.C: Blockchain analysis is unrelated to preventing malware execution on workstations.
whyNot.D: ACLs control access to resources and do not stop unauthorized executables from running.

cards.front:
A network administrator is reviewing the following IDS logs: Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware is triggering the IDS?
A. Trojan
B. Bot
C. Logic Bomb
D. Worm
cards.why: A worm self-replicates and spreads across the network without user action, which produces the repeated propagation pattern an IDS flags.

whyNot.A: A Trojan relies on user execution and does not self-propagate across hosts.
whyNot.B: A bot generates command-and-control and attack traffic, not self-propagating scanning.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb triggers on a condition and does not spread over the network.

cards.front:
A security analyst is checking the bash command history on a Linux host that was involved in a data breach. The data breach stemmed from the Linux host running a series of commands against a web server on the internal network, which exploited a vulnerability in an unpatched Apache module. Given this scenario, which of the following commands might the analyst find in the bash command history for banner grabbing? (Select Three)
A. Arp
B. Tracert
C. NMAP
D. Net Cat (NC)
E. Telnet
F. Grep
G. Nslookup
H. Netstat
cards.back:
C. NMAP
D. Net Cat (NC)
E. Telnet
cards.why: Banner grabbing connects to a service and reads the identifying banner it returns. Nmap (service/version detection), Netcat, and Telnet can all open a connection to a port such as 80 and show the Apache banner.

whyNot.A: Arp displays or manipulates the IP-to-MAC address cache and never queries a service banner.
whyNot.B: Tracert maps the hop-by-hop network path to a host and does not read service banners.
whyNot.F: Grep searches text for patterns and cannot connect to a remote service.
whyNot.G: Nslookup queries DNS records and does not retrieve banners from a web server.
whyNot.H: Netstat lists local connections and listening ports but does not probe remote services for banners.

cards.front:
Which of the following would a security specialist be able to determine upon examination of a server's certificate?
A. CA public key
B. Server private key
C. CSR
D. OID
cards.why: A certificate carries X.509 fields and extensions that contain Object Identifiers (OIDs), such as the signature algorithm and policy identifiers, so an examiner can read them directly.

whyNot.A: The certificate holds the server's public key and the CA's signature, not the CA's public key, which comes from the CA's own certificate.
whyNot.B: The private key is never placed in a certificate and stays secret on the server.
whyNot.C: A CSR is a separate request sent to the CA before issuance and is not contained in the issued certificate.

cards.front:
A security analyst is diagnosing an incident in which a system was compromised from an external IP address. The socket identified on the firewall was traced to 207.46.130.0:6666. Which of the following should the security analyst do to determine if the compromised system still has an active connection?
A. tracert
B. netstat
C. ping
D. nslookup
cards.why: netstat lists active connections and listening sockets with remote addresses and ports, so the analyst can see whether 207.46.130.0:6666 is still established.

whyNot.A: tracert shows the hop path to a destination, not the state of connections on the local system.
whyNot.C: ping tests reachability using ICMP and says nothing about active sockets.
whyNot.D: nslookup resolves DNS names and does not show connection state.

cards.front:
Multiple organizations operating in the same vertical want to provide seamless wireless access for their employees as they visit the other organizations. Which of the following should be implemented if all the organizations use the native 802.1x client on their mobile devices?
A. Shibboleth
B. RADIUS federation
C. SAML
D. OAuth
E. OpenID connect
cards.why: A RADIUS federation lets organizations trust each other's authentication servers, so users can authenticate over 802.1x with their home credentials at any member site, as in eduroam.

whyNot.A: Shibboleth is a web SSO federation system and is not used for native 802.1x wireless authentication.
whyNot.C: SAML exchanges web authentication assertions and is not used by native 802.1x supplicants.
whyNot.D: OAuth is an authorization framework for delegated API access, not network access authentication.
whyNot.E: OpenID Connect is a web authentication layer on OAuth and is not used by native 802.1x clients.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an important security advantage yielded by implementing vendor diversity?
A. Sustainability
B. Homogeneity
C. Resiliency
D. Configurability
cards.why: Vendor diversity means a flaw or outage in one vendor's product does not affect every system, which improves resiliency.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability, not the security benefit of using multiple vendors.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity is the opposite of diversity and creates a single point of failure.
whyNot.D: Configurability is about adjustable settings and is not the main benefit of vendor diversity.

cards.front:
In a corporation where compute utilization spikes several times a year, the Chief Information Officer (CIO) has requested a cost-effective architecture to handle the variable capacity demand. Which of the following characteristics BEST describes what the CIO has requested?
A. Elasticity
B. Scalability
C. High availability
D. Redundancy
cards.back:
A. Elasticity

Elasticity is defined as "the degree to which a system is able to adapt to workload changes by provisioning and de-provisioning resources in an autonomic manner, such that at each point in time the available resources match the current demand as closely as pos...
cards.why: Elasticity is the ability to automatically provision and release resources as demand rises and falls, which is cost-effective for occasional spikes.

whyNot.A: Elasticity is the keyed answer.
whyNot.B: Scalability means the system can grow to handle more load but does not imply releasing capacity afterward to save cost.
whyNot.C: High availability aims to minimize downtime and does not address variable capacity cost.
whyNot.D: Redundancy duplicates components for fault tolerance and does not match demand dynamically.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a system that requires the X.509 certificate information to be pasted into a form field in Base64 encoded format to import it into the system. Which of the following certificate formats should the engineer use to obtain the information in the required format?
A. PFX
B. PEM
C. DER
D. CER
cards.why: PEM is a Base64-encoded text format with BEGIN CERTIFICATE and END CERTIFICATE headers, which can be pasted into a form field.

whyNot.A: PFX (PKCS#12) is a binary container that usually bundles the certificate and private key.
whyNot.C: DER is a binary encoding and cannot be pasted as text.
whyNot.D: CER is an extension that can hold either DER or PEM data and does not guarantee Base64 text.

cards.front:
Which of the following attacks specifically impacts data availability?
A. DDoS
B. Trojan
C. MITM
D. Rootkit
cards.why: A DDoS attack overwhelms a service with traffic from many sources, making it unavailable to legitimate users, which is an attack on availability.

whyNot.B: A Trojan disguises malware to give an attacker access and mainly threatens confidentiality or integrity.
whyNot.C: A MITM attack intercepts or alters traffic, targeting confidentiality and integrity rather than availability.
whyNot.D: A rootkit hides malicious presence and persistence, and it is not designed to deny service.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a server with the directory services role installed. The analyst must ensure LDAP traffic cannot be monitored or sniffed and maintains compatibility with LDAP clients. Which of the following should the analyst implement to meet these requirements? (Select two.)
A. Generate an X.509-compliant certificate that is signed by a trusted CA.
B. Install and configure an SSH tunnel on the LDAP server.
C. Ensure port 389 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
D. Ensure port 636 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
E. Remote the LDAP directory service role from the server.
cards.back:
A. Generate an X.509-compliant certificate that is signed by a trusted CA.
D. Ensure port 636 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
cards.why: Securing LDAP with TLS (LDAPS) requires a certificate signed by a trusted CA, and LDAPS uses port 636, which keeps compatibility with standard LDAP clients.

whyNot.B: An SSH tunnel is a nonstandard workaround that standard LDAP clients are not configured to use.
whyNot.C: Port 389 carries cleartext LDAP, which can be sniffed.
whyNot.E: Removing the directory services role would disable the service the analyst is hardening.

cards.front:
Which of the following threat actors is MOST likely to steal a company's proprietary information to gain a market edge and reduce time to market?
A. Competitor
B. Hacktivist
C. Insider
D. Organized crime.
cards.why: A competitor is motivated by market advantage and shortened development time, so it targets proprietary information such as trade secrets.

whyNot.B: Hacktivists are driven by political or social causes, not market advantage.
whyNot.C: Insiders may steal data for many reasons, but the stated market-edge motive best matches a competitor.
whyNot.D: Organized crime is primarily motivated by direct financial gain, such as ransom or resale of data.

cards.front:
A penetration tester is crawling a target website that is available to the public. Which of the following represents the actions the penetration tester is performing?
A. URL hijacking
B. Reconnaissance
C. White box testing
D. Escalation of privilege
cards.why: Crawling a public website to collect information about the target is reconnaissance, the information-gathering phase of a penetration test.

whyNot.A: URL hijacking (typosquatting) abuses misspelled domain names and is not crawling a target site.
whyNot.C: White box testing means testing with full internal knowledge, while crawling a public site uses only public information.
whyNot.D: Privilege escalation means gaining higher access after a foothold, and crawling does not do that.

cards.keyDoubt: A: Precomputed tables are what make a rainbow table attack differ from brute force, since they cut compute cycles at attack time, while E also applies to offline brute force.

cards.front:
Which of the following characteristics differentiate a rainbow table attack from a brute force attack? (Select two.)
A. Rainbow table attacks greatly reduce compute cycles at attack time.
B. Rainbow tables must include precomputed hashes.
C. Rainbow table attacks do not require access to hashed passwords.
D. Rainbow table attacks must be performed on the network.
E. Rainbow table attacks bypass maximum failed login restrictions.
cards.back:
B. Rainbow tables must include precomputed hashes.
E. Rainbow table attacks bypass maximum failed login restrictions.

cards.front:
Which of the following best describes routine in which semicolons, dashes, quotes, and commas are removed from a string?
A. Error handling to protect against program exploitation
B. Exception handling to protect against XSRF attacks.
C. Input validation to protect against SQL injection.
D. Padding to protect against string buffer overflows.
cards.back: C. Input validation to protect against SQL injection.
cards.why: Stripping characters like semicolons, quotes, dashes, and commas is input validation or sanitization, which blocks SQL injection payloads.

whyNot.A: Error handling controls how failures are reported and does not remove characters from input.
whyNot.B: Exception handling does not sanitize input, and XSRF is prevented with anti-forgery tokens.
whyNot.D: Padding relates to buffer sizing and does not remove special characters.

cards.front:
A security analyst wishes to increase the security of an FTP server. Currently, all traffic to the FTP server is unencrypted. Users connecting to the FTP server use a variety of modern FTP client software. The security analyst wants to keep the same port and protocol, while also still allowing unencrypted connections. Which of the following would BEST accomplish these goals?
A. Require the SFTP protocol to connect to the file server.
B. Use implicit TLS on the FTP server.
C. Use explicit FTPS for connections.
D. Use SSH tunneling to encrypt the FTP traffic.
cards.back: C. Use explicit FTPS for connections.
cards.why: Explicit FTPS (FTPES) starts on the standard FTP port 21 and upgrades to TLS using AUTH TLS, so it can still accept unencrypted clients.

whyNot.A: SFTP is a different protocol that uses SSH on port 22 and cannot keep the same port and protocol.
whyNot.B: Implicit TLS uses a separate port (990) and requires encryption from the start, so it does not allow unencrypted connections.
whyNot.D: SSH tunneling encrypts the traffic but changes how clients connect, and it does not preserve unencrypted access on the same port.

cards.front:
Which of the following explains why vendors publish MD5 values when they provide software patches for their customers to download over the Internet?
A. The recipient can verify integrity of the software patch.
B. The recipient can verify the authenticity of the site used to download the patch.
C. The recipient can request future updates to the software using the published MD5 value.
D. The recipient can successfully activate the new software patch.
cards.back: A. The recipient can verify integrity of the software patch.
cards.why: Comparing the published hash with one computed on the downloaded file verifies integrity, showing the file was not corrupted or altered.

whyNot.B: A hash of the file does not prove the download site is genuine, since an attacker could publish a matching hash.
whyNot.C: Hash values are not used to request updates.
whyNot.D: Activation depends on license keys, not on a file hash.

cards.front:
Refer to the following code: Which of the following vulnerabilities would occur if this is executed?
A. Page exception
B. Pointer deference
C. NullPointerException
D. Missing null check
cards.why: The code was not shown, so this relies on the key: the flaw is that the program uses a reference without first checking it for null, which is a missing null check.

whyNot.A: A page exception is a memory-management fault and not the coding flaw itself.
whyNot.B: Pointer dereference is the operation that fails, while the underlying vulnerability is the absent check.
whyNot.C: NullPointerException is the runtime error produced by the flaw, not the vulnerability.

cards.front:
Multiple employees receive an email with a malicious attachment that begins to encrypt their hard drives and mapped shares on their devices when it is opened. The network and security teams perform the following actions: Shut down all network shares. Run an email search identifying all employees who received the malicious message. Reimage all devices belonging to users who opened the attachment. Next, the teams want to re-enable the network shares. Which of the following BEST describes this phase of the incident response process?
A. Eradication
B. Containment
C. Recovery
D. Lessons learned
cards.why: Recovery restores affected systems and services to normal operation. Re-enabling network shares after the devices are reimaged and the threat is removed is a recovery step.

whyNot.A: Eradication removes the threat, which the reimaging already did; re-enabling shares comes after that.
whyNot.B: Containment limits spread, which shutting down the shares and identifying recipients already accomplished.
whyNot.D: Lessons learned is the post-incident review, not the restoration of services.

cards.front:
An organization has determined it can tolerate a maximum of three hours of downtime. Which of the following has been specified?
A. RTO
B. RPO
C. MTBF
D. MTTR
cards.why: The Recovery Time Objective is the maximum tolerable downtime before a system or process must be restored. A three-hour downtime limit is an RTO.

whyNot.B: RPO specifies the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, not the allowed downtime.
whyNot.C: MTBF is the average time between failures and measures reliability, not tolerated downtime.
whyNot.D: MTTR is the average time needed to repair a failed system, not the business-defined limit.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of keys is found in a key escrow?
A. Public
B. Private
C. Shared
D. Session
cards.why: Key escrow stores private keys with a trusted third party so encrypted data can be recovered if the owner loses the key or is unavailable.

whyNot.A: Public keys are meant to be distributed openly and do not need to be escrowed.
whyNot.C: Shared (symmetric) keys are typically exchanged or derived per use and are not what escrow is defined around.
whyNot.D: Session keys are temporary and discarded after the session, so they are not escrowed.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing the following output from an IPS: Given this output, which of the following can be concluded? (Select two.)
A. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.22.
B. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.71.
C. The attacker sent a malformed IGAP packet, triggering the alert.
D. The attacker sent a malformed TCP packet, triggering the alert.
E. The TTL value is outside of the expected range, triggering the alert.
cards.back:
B. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.71.
C. The attacker sent a malformed IGAP packet, triggering the alert.
cards.why: Based on the keyed reading of the IPS output, the offending source address is 250.19.18.71 and the alert was triggered by a malformed IGAP packet.

whyNot.A: 250.19.18.22 does not appear as the attack source in the keyed reading of the output.
whyNot.D: The alert identifies the protocol as IGAP, not TCP.
whyNot.E: The alert was triggered by the malformed packet, not by the TTL value being out of range.

cards.front:
Despite having implemented password policies, users continue to set the same weak passwords and reuse old passwords. Which of the following technical controls would help prevent these policy violations? (Select two.)
A. Password expiration
B. Password length
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
E. Password lockout
cards.back:
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
cards.why: Password complexity rules block weak passwords, and password history prevents users from reusing previous passwords. Together they enforce the policy technically.

whyNot.A: Expiration forces periodic changes but does not stop weak or recycled passwords.
whyNot.B: Minimum length makes passwords longer but does not prevent weak patterns or reuse.
whyNot.E: Lockout limits brute-force guessing and does not affect password quality or reuse.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of cloud infrastructures would allow several organizations with similar structures and interests to realize the benefits of shared storage and resources?
A. Private
B. Hybrid
C. Public
D. Community
cards.why: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns or structures, so they split the cost of shared storage and resources.

whyNot.A: A private cloud serves a single organization only.
whyNot.B: A hybrid cloud combines private and public models and is not specifically shared by like-minded organizations.
whyNot.C: A public cloud is open to the general public, not a group with similar interests.

cards.front:
A company is currently using the following configuration: IAS server with certificate-based EAP-PEAP and MSCHAP Unencrypted authentication via PAP A security administrator needs to configure a new wireless setup with the following configurations: PAP authentication method PEAP and EAP provide two-factor authentication Which of the following forms of authentication are being used? (Select two.)
A. PAP
B. PEAP
C. MSCHAP
D. PEAP- MSCHAP
E. EAP
F. EAP-PEAP
cards.why: The existing setup uses PAP for unencrypted authentication and MSCHAP as the inner method tunneled inside certificate-based PEAP.

whyNot.B: PEAP is the tunneling protocol that carries the inner method rather than the authentication method itself.
whyNot.D: PEAP-MSCHAP names the combination, whereas the keyed answer picks MSCHAP as the inner method.
whyNot.E: EAP is the general framework and does not name a specific authentication method in use.
whyNot.F: EAP-PEAP describes the tunnel and not the inner credential authentication being used.

cards.front:
An auditor wants to test the security posture of an organization by running a tool that will display the following: Which of the following commands should be used?
A. nbtstat
B. nc
C. arp
D. ipconfig
cards.why: nbtstat displays NetBIOS over TCP/IP statistics and name tables, which an auditor can use to enumerate NetBIOS information on hosts.

whyNot.B: nc (netcat) opens connections and listeners, so it would not produce this kind of table.
whyNot.C: arp shows IP-to-MAC address mappings, not the keyed NetBIOS output.
whyNot.D: ipconfig shows local interface IP configuration, not NetBIOS names or sessions.

cards.front:
A company determines that it is prohibitively expensive to become compliant with new credit card regulations. Instead, the company decides to purchase insurance to cover the cost of any potential loss. Which of the following is the company doing?
A. Transferring the risk
B. Accepting the risk
C. Avoiding the risk
D. Migrating the risk
cards.why: Buying insurance shifts the financial impact of a potential loss to a third party, which is risk transference.

whyNot.B: Acceptance means bearing the loss without shifting it, but the company buys insurance.
whyNot.C: Avoidance means ceasing the risky activity, which the company is not doing.
whyNot.D: Migrating is not a standard risk response; mitigation would reduce the risk rather than shift it.

cards.front:
A company is using a mobile device deployment model in which employees use their personal devices for work at their own discretion. Some of the problems the company is encountering include the following: There is no standardization. Employees ask for reimbursement for their devices. Employees do not replace their devices often enough to keep them running efficiently. The company does not have enough control over the devices. Which of the following is a deployment model that would help the company overcome these problems?
A. BYOD
B. VDI
C. COPE
D. CYOD
cards.why: Choose Your Own Device lets employees pick from a company-approved list of devices, giving standardization and control while the company can manage purchasing and refresh.

whyNot.A: BYOD is the model already in use that is causing these problems.
whyNot.B: VDI delivers virtual desktops and does not define who owns or selects the mobile device.
whyNot.C: COPE gives employees company-owned devices, which would fix control but not the stated problem of employees choosing devices.

cards.front:
A botnet has hit a popular website with a massive number of GRE-encapsulated packets to perform a DDoS attack. News outlets discover a certain type of refrigerator was exploited and used to send outbound packets to the website that crashed. To which of the following categories does the refrigerator belong?
A. SoC
B. ICS
C. IoT
D. MFD
cards.why: A refrigerator with network connectivity is an Internet of Things device, a common botnet recruit because of weak security.

whyNot.A: A SoC is an integrated chip inside a device, not a device category like this.
whyNot.B: ICS refers to industrial control systems that run industrial processes, not consumer appliances.
whyNot.D: An MFD is a multifunction printer/scanner/copier-type device, not a refrigerator.

cards.front:
Users report the following message appears when browsing to the company's secure site: This website cannot be trusted. Which of the following actions should a security analyst take to resolve these messages? (Select two.)
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server.
B. Ensure the certificate has a .pfx extension on the server.
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store.
D. Install the updated private key on the web server.
E. Have users clear their browsing history and relaunch the session.
cards.back:
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server.
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store.
cards.why: An untrusted-site warning usually means the server certificate is expired or the client lacks the issuing root CA. Checking expiration and updating the client root store fix these.

whyNot.B: A .pfx extension is just a file format and does not affect whether clients trust the certificate.
whyNot.D: The private key is never exposed to clients and a new one would not fix the trust chain.
whyNot.E: Browsing history has no bearing on certificate validation.

cards.front:
When trying to log onto a company's new ticketing system, some employees receive the following message: Access denied: too many concurrent sessions. The ticketing system was recently installed on a small VM with only the recommended hardware specifications. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause for this error message?
A. Network resources have been exceeded.
B. The software is out of licenses.
C. The VM does not have enough processing power.
D. The firewall is misconfigured.
cards.back: C. The VM does not have enough processing power.
cards.why: The system was installed on a small VM with only the recommended specs, so limited processing power would cause it to reject sessions under concurrent load.

whyNot.A: Network resource exhaustion would show as slowness or timeouts and not a session-limit denial.
whyNot.B: A license limit is plausible, but nothing in the scenario points to licensing and the hardware detail is the clue.
whyNot.D: A misconfigured firewall would block connections outright rather than cause a concurrent-session message.

cards.front:
Joe, an employee, wants to show his colleagues how much he knows about smartphones. Joe demonstrates a free movie application that he installed from a third party on his corporate smartphone. Joe's colleagues were unable to find the application in the app stores. Which of the following allowed Joe to install the application? (Select two.)
A. Near-field communication.
B. Rooting/jailbreaking
C. Ad-hoc connections
D. Tethering
E. Sideloading
cards.why: Rooting or jailbreaking removes OS restrictions, and sideloading installs apps from outside official stores. Together they let Joe install an unavailable third-party app.

whyNot.A: NFC is a short-range wireless technology for data exchange and does not install apps from outside the store.
whyNot.C: Ad-hoc connections are peer-to-peer wireless links, not an app installation method.
whyNot.D: Tethering shares a device's internet connection and does not bypass app store restrictions.

cards.front:
Which of the following can be provided to an AAA system for the identification phase?
A. Username
B. Permissions
C. One-time token
D. Private certificate
cards.why: Identification is the claim of who you are, which is done by presenting a username. Authentication then proves it.

whyNot.B: Permissions are assigned during authorization, after identity is established.
whyNot.C: A one-time token is a credential used for authentication, not identification.
whyNot.D: A private certificate is an authentication factor proving possession, not the identity claim itself.

cards.front:
Which of the following implements two-factor authentication?
A. A phone system requiring a PIN to make a call
B. At ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
C. A computer requiring username and password
D. A datacenter mantrap requiring fingerprint and iris scan
cards.back: B. At ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
cards.why: An ATM card is something you have and the PIN is something you know, so two different factor categories are combined, which is true two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A PIN alone is a single factor (something you know).
whyNot.C: Username and password are both something you know, so this is single-factor.
whyNot.D: Fingerprint and iris are both biometrics (something you are), so this is one factor type used twice.

cards.front:
Malicious traffic from an internal network has been detected on an unauthorized port on an application server. Which of the following network-based security controls should the engineer consider implementing?
A. ACLs
B. HIPS
C. NAT
D. MAC filtering
cards.why: Network ACLs on a router, firewall, or switch can block traffic on unauthorized ports, which directly addresses malicious traffic on an unapproved port.

whyNot.B: HIPS is host-based, not a network-based control, so it does not fit the question.
whyNot.C: NAT translates addresses and does not filter traffic by port or intent.
whyNot.D: MAC filtering restricts devices by hardware address and cannot block specific ports.

cards.front:
A network administrator wants to implement a method of securing internal routing. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. DMZ
B. NAT
C. VPN
D. PAT
cards.why: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel that protects routing traffic between internal networks, securing it from interception or tampering.

whyNot.A: A DMZ isolates public-facing servers and does not secure internal routing.
whyNot.B: NAT translates addresses and provides no encryption or authentication for routing.
whyNot.D: PAT is a form of NAT mapping ports and does not secure routing traffic.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing controls for creating audit trails and tracking if a PHI data breach is to occur. The administrator has been given the following requirements: All access must be correlated to a user account. All user accounts must be assigned to a single individual. User access to the PHI data must be recorded. Anomalies in PHI data access must be reported. Logs and records cannot be deleted or modified. Which of the following should the administrator implement to meet the above requirements? (Select three.)
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
B. Create a standard naming convention for accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
D. Enable account lockout thresholds.
E. Copy logs in real time to a secured WORM drive.
F. Implement time-of-day restrictions.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.back:
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
