cards.why: Eliminating shared accounts ties activity to individuals, usage auditing and review records and flags anomalous PHI access, and regular permission audits keep access tied to authorized users.

whyNot.B: A naming convention aids organization but does not enforce accountability or record access.
whyNot.D: Lockout thresholds mitigate password guessing and do not meet any listed requirement.
whyNot.E: WORM storage does meet the immutable-log requirement, but the key selects the other three controls.
whyNot.F: Time-of-day restrictions limit when access occurs and do not create audit trails.

cards.keyDoubt: E: The requirement that logs cannot be deleted or modified is met directly by copying logs to WORM storage, while permission audits (G) do not address any stated requirement.

cards.front:
Which of the following encryption methods does PKI typically use to securely protect keys?
A. Elliptic curve
B. Digital signatures
C. Asymmetric
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: PKI uses asymmetric cryptography, where a public/private key pair protects and exchanges keys, such as encrypting a symmetric session key with a public key.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is a specific asymmetric algorithm family, not the general method PKI relies on.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authenticity and integrity, not encryption of keys.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides data without real cryptographic protection and is not used to protect PKI keys.

cards.front:
An organization is using a tool to perform a source code review. Which of the following describes the case in which the tool incorrectly identifies the vulnerability?
A. False negative
B. True negative
C. False positive
D. True positive
cards.why: A false positive is when a tool reports a vulnerability that does not actually exist, which is an incorrect identification.

whyNot.A: A false negative means the tool missed a real vulnerability.
whyNot.B: A true negative means the tool correctly found no vulnerability.
whyNot.D: A true positive means the tool correctly identified a real vulnerability.

cards.front:
An organization's internal auditor discovers that large sums of money have recently been paid to a vendor that management does not recognize. The IT security department is asked to investigate the organization's ERP system to determine how the accounts payable module has been used to make these vendor payments. The IT security department finds the following security configuration for the accounts payable module: New Vendor Entry - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk New Vendor Approval - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk Vendor Payment Entry - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk Vendor Payment Approval - Required Role: Accounts Payable Manager Which of the following changes to the security configuration of the accounts payable module would BEST mitigate the risk?
A. 
B. 
C. 
D.

A department head at a university resigned on the first day of the spring semester. It was subsequently determined that the department head deleted numerous files and directories from the server-based home directory while the campus was closed. Which of the following policies or procedures could have prevented this from occurring?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Permission auditing and review
C. Offboarding
D. Account expiration
cards.why: Offboarding procedures disable accounts and revoke access when an employee leaves, which would have stopped the resigned department head from deleting files.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions would not stop access during hours when the account was otherwise permitted.
whyNot.B: Permission audits review access periodically and would not act at the moment of resignation.
whyNot.D: Account expiration applies to preset dates and does not respond to an unplanned resignation.

cards.front:
A database backup schedule consists of weekly full backups performed on Saturday at 12:00 a.m. and daily differential backups also performed at 12:00 a.m. If the database is restored on Tuesday afternoon, which of the following is the number of individual backups that would need to be applied to complete the database recovery?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 4
cards.why: Restoring requires the last full backup (Saturday) plus the most recent differential (Monday), since differentials are cumulative from the last full backup, for 2 backups.

whyNot.A: One backup would restore only the full backup, missing changes made since Saturday.
whyNot.C: Three would be needed only with incremental backups, where each day is applied in sequence.
whyNot.D: Four would apply every daily backup, which is unnecessary with cumulative differentials.

cards.front:
Which of the following security controls does an iris scanner provide?
A. Logical
B. Administrative
C. Corrective
D. Physical
E. Detective
F. Deterrent
cards.why: An iris scanner physically restricts access to a space or device, making it a physical control, even though it uses biometrics.

whyNot.A: Logical controls are software or technical mechanisms such as ACLs, not a hardware scanner restricting entry.
whyNot.B: Administrative controls are policies and procedures, not devices.
whyNot.C: Corrective controls fix damage after an incident, which a scanner does not do.
whyNot.E: Detective controls identify events after the fact, while a scanner prevents entry.
whyNot.F: Deterrent controls discourage behavior, whereas the scanner actively enforces access.

cards.front:
As part of a new industry regulation, companies are required to utilize secure, standardized OS settings. A technical must ensure the OS settings are hardened. Which of the following is the BEST way to do this?
A. Use a vulnerability scanner.
B. Use a configuration compliance scanner.
C. Use a passive, in-line scanner.
D. Use a protocol analyzer.
cards.back: B. Use a configuration compliance scanner.
cards.why: A configuration compliance scanner checks OS settings against a standardized hardening baseline, such as CIS or STIG, and reports deviations.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner finds missing patches and flaws, not baseline configuration compliance.
whyNot.C: A passive in-line scanner observes traffic and does not assess OS settings.
whyNot.D: A protocol analyzer captures and inspects network packets, not host configuration.

cards.front:
A user has attempted to access data at a higher classification level than the user's account is currently authorized to access. Which of the following access control models has been applied to this user's account?
A. MAC
B. DAC
C. RBAC
D. ABAC
cards.why: Mandatory access control enforces classification labels set by the system, denying users access to data above their clearance level.

whyNot.B: DAC lets data owners grant access at their discretion and does not rely on classification levels.
whyNot.C: RBAC grants access by job role, not by classification clearance.
whyNot.D: ABAC evaluates attributes and policies, not strictly hierarchical classification labels.

cards.front:
A security consultant discovers that an organization is using the PCL protocol to print documents, utilizing the default driver and print settings. Which of the following is the MOST likely risk in this situation?
A. An attacker can access and change the printer configuration.
B. SNMP data leaving the printer will not be properly encrypted.
C. An MITM attack can reveal sensitive information.
D. An attacker can easily inject malicious code into the printer firmware.
E. Attackers can use the PCL protocol to bypass the firewall of client computers.
cards.back: B. SNMP data leaving the printer will not be properly encrypted.
cards.why: PCL printing with default settings leaves printer management traffic such as SNMP unencrypted, so data leaving the printer can be read in transit.

whyNot.A: Changing configuration requires access to the management interface, which is not implied by default PCL use.
whyNot.C: An MITM attack is possible, but the more specific default-setting risk is unencrypted SNMP data.
whyNot.D: Firmware injection is not a typical consequence of using PCL with default drivers.
whyNot.E: PCL is a print language and does not provide a way to bypass client firewalls.

cards.keyDoubt: C: PCL print jobs are sent unencrypted by default, so an MITM attack can capture sensitive document content, which is the most likely risk.

cards.front:
An organization finds that most help desk calls are regarding account lockout due to a variety of applications running on different systems. Management is looking for a solution to reduce the number of account lockouts while improving security. Which of the following is the BEST solution for this organization?
A. Create multiple application accounts for each user.
B. Provide secure tokens.
C. Implement SSO.
D. Utilize role-based access control.
cards.why: Single sign-on lets users authenticate once for many applications, which reduces password-related lockouts while allowing centralized, stronger authentication.

whyNot.A: Multiple accounts per user increase credentials to manage and the lockouts that follow.
whyNot.B: Secure tokens add a factor but do not reduce lockouts across many systems.
whyNot.D: RBAC manages permissions and does not reduce authentication lockouts.

cards.front:
A user suspects someone has been accessing a home network without permission by spoofing the MAC address of an authorized system. While attempting to determine if an authorized user is logged into the home network, the user reviews the wireless router, which shows the following table for systems that are currently on the home network. Which of the following should be the NEXT step to determine if there is an unauthorized user on the network?
A. Apply MAC filtering and see if the router drops any of the systems.
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network.
C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host.
D. Conduct a ping sweep of each of the authorized systems and see if an echo response is received.
cards.back: C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host.
cards.why: The unknown host with no known hostname and no MAC filtering applied is suspicious, so denying it is the direct next step to find out whether it is an intruder.

whyNot.A: MAC filtering is ineffective here because the attacker is spoofing an authorized MAC address.
whyNot.B: Physically checking every system is slow and unnecessary before acting on the unknown host.
whyNot.D: A ping sweep shows only whether systems respond and cannot distinguish a spoofed MAC.

cards.keyDoubt: B: A spoofed MAC is indistinguishable at the router, so physically verifying each authorized device is the reliable way to find a duplicate.

cards.front:
When performing data acquisition on a workstation, which of the following should be captured based on memory volatility? (Select two.)
A. USB-attached hard disk
B. Swap/pagefile
C. Mounted network storage
D. ROM
E. RAM
cards.why: Order of volatility puts RAM first, then swap/pagefile, which holds memory contents on disk and changes while the system runs, so both must be captured early.

whyNot.A: A USB-attached hard disk is persistent storage and far less volatile.
whyNot.C: Mounted network storage is persistent and held remotely, so it is lower priority.
whyNot.D: ROM is non-volatile and does not change.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, has been instructed to perform fuzz-based testing on the company's applications. Which of the following best describes what she will do?
A. Enter random or invalid data into the application in an attempt to cause it to fault
B. Work with the developers to eliminate horizontal privilege escalation opportunities
C. Test the applications for the existence of built-in- back doors left by the developers
D. Hash the application to verify it won't cause a false positive on the HIPS.
cards.back: A. Enter random or invalid data into the application in an attempt to cause it to fault
cards.why: Fuzzing feeds random, malformed, or unexpected input to an application to trigger crashes or faults and expose input-handling vulnerabilities.

whyNot.B: Eliminating horizontal privilege escalation is an access-control and code-review task, not fuzzing.
whyNot.C: Finding built-in back doors requires code review or reverse engineering, not random input testing.
whyNot.D: Hashing an application for HIPS allow-listing is integrity verification, unrelated to fuzzing.

cards.front:
An attacker compromises a public CA and issues unauthorized X.509 certificates for Company.com. In the future, Company.com wants to mitigate the impact of similar incidents. Which of the following would assist Company.com with its goal?
A. Certificate pinning
B. Certificate stapling
C. Certificate chaining
D. Certificate with extended validation
cards.why: Certificate pinning binds a host to a specific certificate or public key, so a fraudulent certificate issued by a compromised public CA will be rejected.

whyNot.B: Stapling delivers OCSP revocation status but does not stop a validly signed fraudulent certificate from being trusted.
whyNot.C: Chaining is the trust path from a certificate up to the root and does not limit which certificates are accepted.
whyNot.D: Extended validation adds identity vetting, but a compromised CA can still issue unauthorized certificates that clients trust.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is attempting to recover from a catastrophic failure in the datacenter. To recover the domain controller, the systems administrator needs to provide the domain administrator credentials. Which of the following account types is the systems administrator using?
A. Shared account
B. Guest account
C. Service account
D. User account
cards.why: Recovering a domain controller in this scenario relies on a privileged account used by the system or a service, which matches a service account; the key says C.

whyNot.A: A shared account is used by multiple people and is not what the key indicates here.
whyNot.B: A guest account has minimal privileges and could not supply domain administrator rights.
whyNot.D: A standard user account lacks the privileges needed for domain controller recovery.

cards.keyDoubt: A domain administrator credential used by a person is more naturally a privileged user account (D), though the key follows the service-account reading.

cards.front:
A security administrator has found a hash in the environment known to belong to malware. The administrator then finds this file to be in in the preupdate area of the OS, which indicates it was pushed from the central patch system. File: winx86_adobe_flash_upgrade.exe Hash: 99ac28bede43ab869b853ba62c4ea243 The administrator pulls a report from the patch management system with the following output: Given the above outputs, which of the following MOST likely happened?
A. The file was corrupted after it left the patch system.
B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it.
C. The file was not approved in the application whitelist system.
D. The file was embedded with a logic bomb to evade detection.
cards.back: B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it.
cards.why: The malware hash matches the file in the patch system's pre-update area, which indicates the file was already malicious when the patch manager downloaded it from the source.

whyNot.A: Corruption after leaving the patch system would produce a hash mismatch rather than a known-malware hash match.
whyNot.C: Whitelist approval status does not explain how the malicious file came to exist in the patch repository.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is code that triggers on a condition and does not explain a hash already known as malware.

cards.front:
A network administrator at a small office wants to simplify the configuration of mobile clients connecting to an encrypted wireless network. Which of the following should be implemented if the administrator does not want to provide the wireless password or the certificate to the employees?
A. WPS
B. 802.1x
C. WPA2-PSK
D. TKIP
cards.why: WPS lets clients join an encrypted wireless network through a PIN or push button without the user being given the passphrase or a certificate.

whyNot.B: 802.1X requires each client to have credentials or certificates, which the administrator does not want to distribute.
whyNot.C: WPA2-PSK requires users to know the shared wireless password.
whyNot.D: TKIP is a legacy encryption protocol and does not simplify client onboarding.

cards.front:
When connected to a secure WAP, which of the following encryption technologies is MOST likely to be configured when connecting to WPA2-PSK?
A. DES
B. AES
C. MD5
D. WEP
cards.why: WPA2 uses AES with CCMP for encryption, so AES is the technology configured with WPA2-PSK.

whyNot.A: DES is an obsolete cipher and is not used by WPA2.
whyNot.C: MD5 is a hashing algorithm, not a wireless encryption technology.
whyNot.D: WEP is a separate, older, insecure wireless protocol that predates WPA2.

cards.front:
A company has a data classification system with definitions for "Private" and "Public". The company's security policy outlines how data should be protected based on type. The company recently added the data type "Proprietary". Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the company added this data type?
A. Reduced cost
B. More searchable data
C. Better data classification
D. Expanded authority of the privacy officer
cards.why: Adding a more specific data type such as Proprietary gives finer granularity, which improves data classification and lets policy apply protections more precisely.

whyNot.A: Adding a classification tier does not by itself reduce cost and may increase handling overhead.
whyNot.B: Classification labels do not make data more searchable.
whyNot.D: Adding a data type does not expand the privacy officer's authority.

cards.front:
When configuring settings in a mandatory access control environment, which of the following specifies the subjects that can access specific data objects?
A. Owner
B. System
C. Administrator
D. User
cards.why: In mandatory access control, the administrator configures the policy and labels that determine which subjects may access which objects; owners and users cannot change them.

whyNot.A: Owners set permissions in discretionary access control, not mandatory access control.
whyNot.B: The system enforces the policy but the administrator is the one who defines it.
whyNot.D: Users are subjects constrained by the policy and cannot specify access.

cards.front:
A high-security defense installation recently begun utilizing large guard dogs that bark very loudly and excitedly at the slightest provocation. Which of the following types of controls does this BEST describe?
A. Deterrent
B. Preventive
C. Detective
D. Compensating
cards.why: Loud, aggressive guard dogs discourage potential intruders from attempting entry, which makes them a deterrent control.

whyNot.B: Preventive controls physically block access, such as locks or fences, rather than discouraging it.
whyNot.C: Detective controls identify an event after or as it occurs, and the question stresses discouragement.
whyNot.D: Compensating controls substitute for another control that cannot be implemented, which is not described.

cards.front:
A company's user lockout policy is enabled after five unsuccessful login attempts. The help desk notices a user is repeatedly locked out over the course of a workweek. Upon contacting the user, the help desk discovers the user is on vacation and does not have network access. Which of the following types of attacks are MOST likely occurring? (Choose two.)
A. Replay
B. Rainbow tables
C. Brute force
D. Pass the hash
E. Dictionary
cards.why: Repeated lockouts while the user is away indicate someone is guessing passwords against the account, which fits brute force and dictionary attacks.

whyNot.A: Replay attacks resend captured authentication data and would not cause repeated failed-password lockouts.
whyNot.B: Rainbow tables are used offline against stolen hashes and do not generate online failed logins.
whyNot.D: Pass the hash reuses a captured hash and does not produce repeated failed password attempts.

cards.front:
Ann, an employee in the payroll department, has contacted the help desk citing multiple issues with her device, including: Slow performance Word documents, PDFs, and images no longer opening A pop-up Ann states the issues began after she opened an invoice that a vendor emailed to her. Upon opening the invoice, she had to click several security warnings to view it in her word processor. With which of the following is the device MOST likely infected?
A. Spyware
B. Crypto-malware
C. Rootkit
D. Backdoor
cards.why: Files that no longer open combined with a ransom-style pop-up after enabling macros in an emailed invoice points to crypto-malware (ransomware) encrypting documents; the key says D.

whyNot.A: Spyware gathers information quietly and does not make documents unopenable.
whyNot.B: Crypto-malware is listed as wrong by the key, though it fits the encrypted files best.
whyNot.C: A rootkit hides malicious activity and does not make files unreadable.

cards.keyDoubt: B, because unopenable documents plus a pop-up after enabling an invoice's macros are classic signs of crypto-malware, not a backdoor.

cards.front:
A company is terminating an employee for misbehavior. Which of the following steps is MOST important in the process of disengagement from this employee?
A. Obtain a list of passwords used by the employee.
B. Generate a report on outstanding projects the employee handled.
C. Have the employee surrender company identification.
D. Have the employee sign an NDA before departing.
cards.back: C. Have the employee surrender company identification.
cards.why: Collecting company identification and badges removes the former employee's physical access, which is the most important immediate step when disengaging a terminated employee.

whyNot.A: Passwords should be reset or disabled by IT rather than collected from the employee.
whyNot.B: A project report is useful for continuity but does not protect security.
whyNot.D: An NDA should be signed at hiring, and a terminated employee may not cooperate.

cards.front:
A company is developing a new secure technology and requires computers being used for development to be isolated. Which of the following should be implemented to provide the MOST secure environment?
A. A perimeter firewall and IDS
B. An air gapped computer network
C. A honeypot residing in a DMZ
D. An ad hoc network with NAT
E. A bastion host
cards.back: B. An air gapped computer network
cards.why: An air-gapped network is physically isolated from other networks, giving the strongest isolation for sensitive development systems.

whyNot.A: A perimeter firewall and IDS still leave the systems connected to other networks.
whyNot.C: A honeypot in a DMZ is a decoy and does not isolate development computers.
whyNot.D: An ad hoc network with NAT remains connected and is not truly isolated.
whyNot.E: A bastion host is an exposed hardened system and does not provide isolation.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an important step to take BEFORE moving any installation packages from a test environment to production?
A. Roll back changes in the test environment
B. Verify the hashes of files
C. Archive and compress the files
D. Update the secure baseline
cards.back: B. Verify the hashes of files
cards.why: Verifying file hashes confirms the packages were not altered or corrupted before they are deployed to production, supporting integrity.

whyNot.A: Rolling back test changes would undo the tested state and does not validate the packages.
whyNot.C: Archiving and compressing files does not verify integrity or safety.
whyNot.D: Updating the secure baseline happens after deployment to reflect the new approved state.

cards.front:
A user clicked an email link that led to a website than infected the workstation with a virus. The virus encrypted all the network shares to which the user had access. The virus was not deleted or blocked by the company's email filter, website filter, or antivirus. Which of the following describes what occurred?
A. The user's account was over-privileged.
B. Improper error handling triggered a false negative in all three controls.
C. The email originated from a private email server with no malware protection.
D. The virus was a zero-day attack.
cards.back: D. The virus was a zero-day attack.
cards.why: Malware that passes the email filter, website filter, and antivirus undetected is consistent with a zero-day attack, since no signatures exist for it yet.

whyNot.A: Over-privilege widened the damage but does not explain why three controls failed to detect the virus.
whyNot.B: Error handling flaws do not explain a false negative simultaneously across three separate controls.
whyNot.C: The email's origin is not established and does not explain the web filter and antivirus failing.

cards.front:
An organization wishes to provide better security for its name resolution services. Which of the following technologies BEST supports the deployment of DNSSEC at the organization?
A. LDAP
B. TPM
C. TLS
D. SSL
E. PKI
cards.why: DNSSEC digitally signs DNS records using public/private key pairs, and PKI provides the key management and trust infrastructure for those signatures.

whyNot.A: LDAP is a directory access protocol and plays no role in signing DNS records.
whyNot.B: A TPM is hardware for local key storage and attestation, not a DNSSEC trust framework.
whyNot.C: TLS secures data in transit between endpoints, while DNSSEC signs the DNS data itself.
whyNot.D: SSL is a deprecated transport encryption protocol and does not provide DNS record signing.

cards.keyDoubt: E. DNSSEC relies on public key signatures and a chain of trust, which is PKI, not TLS.

cards.front:
A company hires a consulting firm to crawl its Active Directory network with a non-domain account looking for unpatched systems. Actively taking control of systems is out of scope, as is the creation of new administrator accounts. For which of the following is the company hiring the consulting firm?
A. Vulnerability scanning
B. Penetration testing
C. Application fuzzing
D. User permission auditing
cards.why: Crawling the network with a non-credentialed account to find unpatched systems, without exploiting them, is vulnerability scanning.

whyNot.B: Penetration testing actively exploits weaknesses and takes control of systems, which is out of scope.
whyNot.C: Fuzzing sends malformed input to an application to find bugs, not to find unpatched systems.
whyNot.D: Permission auditing reviews user rights and access, not patch levels.

cards.front:
An administrator is replacing a wireless router. The configuration of the old wireless router was not documented before it stopped functioning. The equipment connecting to the wireless network uses older legacy equipment that was manufactured prior to the release of the 802.11i standard. Which of the following configuration options should the administrator select for the new wireless router?
A. WPA+CCMP
B. WPA2+CCMP
C. WPA+TKIP
D. WPA2+TKIP
cards.why: Pre-802.11i hardware cannot support WPA2 or CCMP, so WPA with TKIP is the strongest option those legacy devices can use.

whyNot.A: CCMP/AES requires hardware designed for 802.11i, which legacy devices lack.
whyNot.B: WPA2 with CCMP is the 802.11i standard and legacy equipment cannot support it.
whyNot.D: WPA2 normally pairs with CCMP, and legacy hardware predating 802.11i cannot run WPA2.

cards.front:
An application team is performing a load-balancing test for a critical application during off-hours and has requested access to the load balancer to review which servers are up without having the administrator on call. The security analyst is hesitant to give the application team full access due to other critical applications running on the load balancer. Which of the following is the BEST solution for security analyst to process the request?
A. Give the application team administrator access during off-hours.
B. Disable other critical applications before granting the team access.
C. Give the application team read-only access.
D. Share the account with the application team.
cards.back: C. Give the application team read-only access.
cards.why: Read-only access follows least privilege, letting the team see which servers are up without being able to change the other critical applications.

whyNot.A: Administrator access violates least privilege and exposes other critical applications to changes.
whyNot.B: Disabling critical applications causes an outage and is an unreasonable way to grant access.
whyNot.D: Shared accounts destroy accountability and auditing, and are a poor security practice.

cards.front:
Which of the following cryptographic attacks would salting of passwords render ineffective?
A. Brute force
B. Dictionary
C. Rainbow tables
D. Birthday
cards.why: Salting gives each password a unique random value before hashing, so precomputed rainbow tables no longer match and become useless.

whyNot.A: Brute force computes hashes live, and a salt only adds minor per-password work.
whyNot.B: Dictionary attacks can still hash each guess with the salt, so salting does not stop them.
whyNot.D: Birthday attacks target hash collisions, which salting does not prevent.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening an authentication server. One of the primary requirements is to ensure there is mutual authentication and delegation. Given these requirements, which of the following technologies should the analyst recommend and configure?
A. LDAP services
B. Kerberos services
C. NTLM services
D. CHAP services
cards.back:
B. Kerberos services

Only Kerberos that can do Mutual Auth and Delegation.
cards.why: Kerberos uses tickets to provide mutual authentication between client and server, and it supports delegation of credentials to services.

whyNot.A: LDAP is a directory protocol and does not provide mutual authentication with delegation.
whyNot.C: NTLM is a challenge-response protocol that lacks mutual authentication and proper delegation.
whyNot.D: CHAP authenticates only the client to the server and has no delegation.

cards.front:
Two users need to send each other emails over unsecured channels. The system should support the principle of non-repudiation. Which of the following should be used to sign the user's certificates?
A. RA
B. CA
C. CRL
D. CSR
cards.why: A certificate authority signs certificates with its private key, establishing trust in the users' keys and supporting non-repudiation of signed email.

whyNot.A: A registration authority verifies identities but does not sign certificates.
whyNot.C: A CRL lists revoked certificates and does not sign them.
whyNot.D: A CSR is the request a user submits to a CA, not the signer.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types BEST describes a client-side attack that is used to manipulate an HTML iframe with JavaScript code via a web browser?
A. Buffer overflow
B. MITM
C. XSS
D. SQLi
cards.why: Cross-site scripting injects JavaScript that runs in the victim's browser, including manipulating page elements like iframes.

whyNot.A: Buffer overflow exploits memory handling in a program, not browser HTML or iframes.
whyNot.B: MITM intercepts traffic between parties and is not a client-side script manipulation attack.
whyNot.D: SQL injection targets back-end databases, not the browser.

cards.front:
An incident responder receives a call from a user who reports a computer is exhibiting symptoms consistent with a malware infection. Which of the following steps should the responder perform NEXT?
A. Capture and document necessary information to assist in the response.
B. Request the user capture and provide a screenshot or recording of the symptoms.
C. Use a remote desktop client to collect and analyze the malware in real time.
D. Ask the user to back up files for later recovery.
cards.back: A. Capture and document necessary information to assist in the response.
cards.why: After receiving a report, the responder should first capture and document the details, which is the identification step of the incident response process.

whyNot.B: Asking for screenshots is a possible follow-up but not the first step after the report.
whyNot.C: Analyzing malware live on the user's machine risks spreading it and comes later.
whyNot.D: Backing up files from a possibly infected system could spread malware and is premature.

cards.front:
A senior incident response manager receives a call about some external IPs communicating with internal computers during off hours. Which of the following types of malware is MOST likely causing this issue?
A. Botnet
B. Ransomware
C. Polymorphic malware
D. Armored virus
cards.why: External IPs communicating with many internal computers off hours suggests command-and-control traffic from infected machines in a botnet.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment rather than showing quiet external communication.
whyNot.C: Polymorphic malware changes its code to evade detection, which does not explain the traffic pattern.
whyNot.D: Armored viruses resist analysis and do not specifically indicate external C2 communication.

cards.front:
Which of the following technologies employ the use of SAML? (Select two.)
A. Single sign-on
B. Federation
C. LDAP
D. Secure token
E. RADIUS
cards.why: SAML exchanges authentication assertions between identity and service providers, enabling single sign-on and federation across domains.

whyNot.C: LDAP is a directory access protocol and does not use SAML.
whyNot.D: Secure tokens are hardware or software authenticators and are not defined by SAML.
whyNot.E: RADIUS is a separate AAA protocol that does not use SAML.

cards.front:
Which of the following specifically describes the exploitation of an interactive process to access otherwise restricted areas of the OS?
A. Privilege escalation
B. Pivoting
C. Process affinity
D. Buffer overflow
cards.why: Privilege escalation exploits a process or flaw to gain higher access than intended to restricted areas of the operating system.

whyNot.B: Pivoting uses a compromised host to reach other network systems, not elevate rights on one.
whyNot.C: Process affinity binds a process to specific CPUs and is not an attack.
whyNot.D: Buffer overflow is one technique that can enable escalation but does not specifically describe it.

cards.front:
After a user reports slow computer performance, a system administrator detects a suspicious file, which was installed as part of a freeware software package. The systems administrator reviews the output below: Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the user's computer?
A. RAT
B. Keylogger
C. Spyware
D. Worm
E. Bot
cards.why: A RAT gives an attacker remote control of the host and is often bundled with freeware; the key assigns RAT based on the output shown.

whyNot.B: A keylogger only records keystrokes and does not provide remote control.
whyNot.C: Spyware gathers information but does not give remote administrative access.
whyNot.D: A worm self-propagates across the network, which is not indicated here.
whyNot.E: A bot joins a botnet for commanded tasks, which differs from the remote access indicated.

cards.front:
Which of the following network vulnerability scan indicators BEST validates a successful, active scan?
A. The scan job is scheduled to run during off-peak hours.
B. The scan output lists SQL injection attack vectors.
C. The scan data identifies the use of privileged-user credentials.
D. The scan results identify the hostname and IP address.
cards.back: B. The scan output lists SQL injection attack vectors.
cards.why: Finding SQL injection vectors shows the scan actively probed the target and detected exploitable weaknesses, validating an active scan.

whyNot.A: Scheduling only shows when the scan runs, not that it succeeded.
whyNot.C: Privileged credentials indicate a credentialed scan, not whether the scan was active and successful.
whyNot.D: Hostname and IP appear in passive discovery too, so they do not prove active scanning.

cards.front:
An analyst wants to implement a more secure wireless authentication for office access points. Which of the following technologies allows for encrypted authentication of wireless clients over TLS?
A. PEAP
B. EAP
C. WPA2
D. RADIUS
cards.back:
A. PEAP

EAP by itself is only an authentication framework. PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) fully encapsulates EAP and is designed to work within a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel that may be encrypted but is authenticated.
cards.why: PEAP creates an encrypted TLS tunnel to protect the authentication exchange of wireless clients.

whyNot.B: EAP is a framework and does not itself provide a TLS tunnel.
whyNot.C: WPA2 is a wireless security standard, not a TLS-based authentication method.
whyNot.D: RADIUS is the authentication server protocol and does not itself tunnel EAP over TLS.

cards.front:
When systems, hardware, or software are not supported by the original vendor, it is a vulnerability known as:
A. system sprawl
B. end-of-life systems
C. resource exhaustion
D. a default configuration
cards.why: End-of-life systems no longer receive vendor patches or support, so newly discovered flaws stay unfixed. That is a recognized vulnerability category.

whyNot.A: System sprawl is uncontrolled growth of systems that are hard to track, not loss of vendor support.
whyNot.C: Resource exhaustion is depleting CPU, memory, or bandwidth, which is unrelated to vendor support.
whyNot.D: A default configuration is unchanged factory settings, which can be insecure but is not about vendor support ending.

cards.front:
A company has three divisions, each with its own networks and services. The company decides to make its secure web portal accessible to all employees utilizing their existing usernames and passwords. The security administrator has elected to use SAML to support authentication. In this scenario, which of the following will occur when users try to authenticate to the portal? (Select two.)
A. The portal will function as a service provider and request an authentication assertion.
B. The portal will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
C. The portal will request an authentication ticket from each network that is transitively trusted.
D. The back-end networks will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
E. The back-end networks will request authentication tickets from the portal, which will act as the third-party service provider authentication store.
F. The back-end networks will verify the assertion token issued by the portal functioning as the identity provider.
cards.back:
C. The portal will request an authentication ticket from each network that is transitively trusted.
D. The back-end networks will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
cards.why: In SAML, the back-end networks hold the existing credentials, so they act as identity providers that issue authentication assertions (D). The key pairs this with C, a portal pulling authentication from each trusted network.

whyNot.A: This is how SAML actually works, since the portal is the service provider requesting an assertion, though the key does not select it.
whyNot.B: The portal holds no credentials here, so it is the service provider rather than the identity provider.
whyNot.E: The direction is reversed, because the portal asks the back-end networks for assertions rather than the other way around.
whyNot.F: The back-end networks issue the assertions, and the portal as service provider verifies them.

cards.keyDoubt: A rather than C: SAML uses assertions rather than tickets, and the portal acts as service provider requesting an assertion from the back-end identity providers.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST explanation of why control diversity is important in a defense- in-depth architecture?
A. Social engineering is used to bypass technical controls, so having diversity in controls minimizes the risk of demographic exploitation
B. Hackers often impact the effectiveness of more than one control, so having multiple copies of individual controls provides redundancy
C. Technical exploits to defeat controls are released almost every day; control diversity provides overlapping protection.
D. Defense-in-depth relies on control diversity to provide multiple levels of network hierarchy that allow user domain segmentation
cards.back: D. Defense-in-depth relies on control diversity to provide multiple levels of network hierarchy that allow user domain segmentation
cards.why: The keyed answer treats control diversity as layering different control types to create multiple levels of separation. That is a loose fit for the concept.

whyNot.A: Control diversity is not about demographics, and the claim misdescribes the risk.
whyNot.B: Multiple copies of the same control is redundancy, not diversity, and one flaw would defeat every copy.
whyNot.C: This is the best description, since different control types overlap so one exploit cannot defeat every layer, but the key does not select it.

cards.keyDoubt: C because control diversity means using different control types so a single exploit cannot defeat all layers, which is what C describes.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to provide balance between the security of a wireless network and usability. The administrator is concerned with wireless encryption compatibility of older devices used by some employees. Which of the following would provide strong security and backward compatibility when accessing the wireless network?
A. Open wireless network and SSL VPN
B. WPA using a preshared key
C. WPA2 using a RADIUS back-end for 802.1x authentication
D. WEP with a 40-bit key
cards.back: B. WPA using a preshared key
cards.why: WPA with a preshared key works on older hardware that lacks WPA2 or 802.1x support while still encrypting traffic, so it balances compatibility and security.

whyNot.A: An open network gives no wireless encryption, and relying on a VPN alone does not secure the wireless link.
whyNot.C: WPA2 with 802.1x is the strongest option, but older devices may not support it, which is why the key rejects it.
whyNot.D: WEP with a 40-bit key is trivially cracked and provides no meaningful security.

cards.keyDoubt: C because WPA2 with RADIUS and 802.1x gives strong security, and most legacy devices that support WPA can be updated for it.

cards.front:
An information security specialist is reviewing the following output from a Linux server. Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the server?
A. Logic bomb
B. Trojan
C. Backdoor
D. Ransomware
E. Rootkit
cards.why: A logic bomb is code that lies dormant until a condition such as a date or event triggers it. The keyed answer reads the server output as such a trigger-based payload.

whyNot.B: A Trojan masquerades as legitimate software and does not wait on a trigger condition.
whyNot.C: A backdoor provides covert remote access rather than a conditional payload.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, and the output shows no encryption activity.
whyNot.E: A rootkit hides its presence at a low level and does not execute on a trigger condition.

cards.front:
In terms of encrypting data, which of the following is BEST described as a way to safeguard password data by adding random data to it in storage?
A. Using salt
B. Using hash algorithms
C. Implementing elliptical curve
D. Implementing PKI
cards.why: Salting adds random data to a password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes and rainbow tables become ineffective.

whyNot.B: Hashing alone produces identical output for identical passwords and does not add random data.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve cryptography is an asymmetric key technique, not a password storage safeguard.
whyNot.D: PKI manages certificates and key distribution, not password storage.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to provide for and enforce wireless access accountability during events where external speakers are invited to make presentations to a mixed audience of employees and non-employees. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. Shared accounts
B. Preshared passwords
C. Least privilege
D. Sponsored guest
cards.why: A sponsored guest account ties each non-employee's wireless access to an employee sponsor, which enforces accountability for temporary visitors.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts hide individual identity, so they defeat accountability.
whyNot.B: A preshared password is known by everyone and cannot identify individual users.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits permissions but does not create individual accountability for guests.

cards.front:
Which of the following would MOST likely appear in an uncredentialed vulnerability scan?
A. Self-signed certificates
B. Missing patches
C. Auditing parameters
D. Inactive local accounts
cards.why: The key says inactive local accounts, but that is a poor fit because enumerating local accounts requires credentialed access to the host.

whyNot.A: Self-signed certificates are visible to a network scanner without credentials, so this is what an uncredentialed scan would most likely report.
whyNot.B: Missing patches are normally found with credentials, though banner checks can sometimes reveal them remotely.
whyNot.C: Auditing parameters are internal host settings that need credentialed access to read.

cards.keyDoubt: A because an uncredentialed scan sees only what the network exposes, such as certificates, and cannot read local accounts.

cards.front:
A security analyst observes the following events in the logs of an employee workstation: Given the information provided, which of the following MOST likely occurred on the workstation?
A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
B. Antivirus software found and quarantined three malware files.
C. Automatic updates were initiated but failed because they had not been approved.
D. The SIEM log agent was not tuned properly and reported a false positive.
cards.back: A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
cards.why: The keyed answer reads the log entries as application whitelisting blocking an unapproved payload from running, which is an allow-list control at work.

whyNot.B: Antivirus quarantine events would name detected malware files and a quarantine action.
whyNot.C: Update failures would show update service errors rather than blocked executions.
whyNot.D: A SIEM agent tuning problem would not generate these host-level block events.

cards.front:
When identifying a company's most valuable assets as part of a BIA, which of the following should be the FIRST priority?
A. Life
B. Intellectual property
C. Sensitive data
D. Public reputation
cards.why: In a business impact analysis, human life and safety always take priority over every other asset.

whyNot.B: Intellectual property is valuable but ranks below human safety.
whyNot.C: Sensitive data matters for compliance and confidentiality but ranks below life.
whyNot.D: Public reputation can be rebuilt over time and ranks below life.

cards.front:
An organization needs to implement a large PKI. Network engineers are concerned that repeated transmission of the OCSP will impact network performance. Which of the following should the security analyst recommend is lieu of an OCSP?
A. CSR
B. CRL
C. CA
D. OID
cards.why: A certificate revocation list is downloaded periodically and cached, which avoids repeated per-certificate OCSP queries across the network.

whyNot.A: A CSR is a request to obtain a certificate, not a revocation checking method.
whyNot.C: A CA issues certificates and is not a revocation checking mechanism.
whyNot.D: An OID is an identifier for object types and does not check revocation.

cards.front:
When considering a third-party cloud service provider, which of the following criteria would be the BEST to include in the security assessment process? (Select two.)
A. Use of performance analytics
B. Adherence to regulatory compliance
C. Data retention policies
D. Size of the corporation
E. Breadth of applications support
cards.back:
B. Adherence to regulatory compliance
C. Data retention policies
cards.why: Regulatory compliance and data retention policies directly affect how well the provider protects and handles your data, so they belong in a security assessment.

whyNot.A: Performance analytics concerns service quality rather than security posture.
whyNot.D: Corporation size does not indicate how well data is protected.
whyNot.E: Breadth of application support is a functionality factor and not a security criterion.

cards.front:
Which of the following occurs when the security of a web application relies on JavaScript for input validation?
A. The integrity of the data is at risk.
B. The security of the application relies on antivirus.
C. A host-based firewall is required.
D. The application is vulnerable to race conditions.
cards.back: A. The integrity of the data is at risk.
cards.why: Client-side JavaScript validation can be bypassed by sending requests directly or altering the script, so malformed input can reach the server and put data integrity at risk.

whyNot.B: Antivirus does not substitute for server-side input validation.
whyNot.C: A host firewall does not address bypassed input validation in the application layer.
whyNot.D: Race conditions come from timing of concurrent operations and are not caused by client-side validation.

cards.front:
An analyst is reviewing a simple program for potential security vulnerabilities before being deployed to a Windows server. Given the following code: Which of the following vulnerabilities is present?
A. Bad memory pointer
B. Buffer overflow
C. Integer overflow
D. Backdoor
cards.why: The keyed answer identifies a buffer overflow, where input is copied into a fixed-size buffer without a length check and can overwrite adjacent memory.

whyNot.A: A bad memory pointer involves invalid or dangling pointers rather than unchecked copy length.
whyNot.C: An integer overflow comes from arithmetic exceeding a type's range, which the keyed reading does not involve.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is intentionally hidden access and is not a coding error from missing bounds checks.

cards.front:
An organization's file server has been virtualized to reduce costs. Which of the following types of backups would be MOST appropriate for the particular file server?
A. Snapshot
B. Full
C. Incremental
D. Differential
cards.why: The keyed answer chooses incremental backups, which store only changes since the last backup and so save space and time on a file server.

whyNot.A: A snapshot captures the whole virtual machine state at a point in time and is the usual fit for virtualized servers.
whyNot.B: A full backup copies everything each time, which is slow and storage-heavy.
whyNot.D: A differential backup grows with every run, since it copies all changes since the last full backup.

cards.keyDoubt: A because snapshots are the standard fast, hypervisor-level way to back up a virtualized server.

cards.front:
A wireless network uses a RADIUS server that is connected to an authenticator, which in turn connects to a supplicant. Which of the following represents the authentication architecture in use?
A. Open systems authentication
B. Captive portal
C. RADIUS federation
D. 802.1x
cards.why: 802.1X is port-based network access control where a supplicant authenticates through an authenticator to a RADIUS authentication server, matching the described architecture.

whyNot.A: Open system authentication performs no real identity verification and involves no RADIUS server.
whyNot.B: A captive portal redirects users to a web login page and does not use a supplicant/authenticator model.
whyNot.C: RADIUS federation links RADIUS servers across organizations for roaming; it is not the supplicant-authenticator-server architecture.

cards.front:
An employer requires that employees use a key-generating app on their smartphones to log into corporate applications. In terms of authentication of an individual, this type of access policy is BEST defined as:
A. Something you have.
B. Something you know.
C. Something you do.
D. Something you are.
cards.why: A key-generating app on a smartphone is a possession factor, so it is something you have.

whyNot.B: Something you know is a secret like a password or PIN, not a device-generated key.
whyNot.C: Something you do refers to behavioral actions such as gestures or typing patterns.
whyNot.D: Something you are refers to biometrics such as fingerprints or retina scans.

cards.front:
Adhering to a layered security approach, a controlled access facility employs security guards who verify the authorization of all personnel entering the facility. Which of the following terms BEST describes the security control being employed?
A. Administrative
B. Corrective
C. Deterrent
D. Compensating
cards.why: Guards verifying authorization are a human-driven procedure, but the key labels this administrative; the closest fit among the options is administrative, which governs people through policy and procedure.

whyNot.B: Corrective controls restore systems after an incident, which guards checking entry do not do.
whyNot.C: Deterrent controls discourage attempts, whereas the guards actively verify authorization.
whyNot.D: Compensating controls substitute for a primary control that cannot be implemented, which is not described.

cards.keyDoubt: C. Guards verifying authorization are physical controls, and among the listed types they are best viewed as preventive/deterrent, though administrative is arguable if the key treats procedures as policy-driven.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a web server, which should allow a secure certificate-based session using the organization's PKI infrastructure. The web server should also utilize the latest security techniques and standards. Given this set of requirements, which of the following techniques should the analyst implement to BEST meet these requirements? (Select two.)
A. Install an X- 509-compliant certificate.
B. Implement a CRL using an authorized CA.
C. Enable and configure TLS on the server.
D. Install a certificate signed by a public CA.
E. Configure the web server to use a host header.
cards.back:
A. Install an X- 509-compliant certificate.
C. Enable and configure TLS on the server.
cards.why: An X.509 certificate is the standard format for PKI-based certificates, and TLS is the current protocol that provides the secure, certificate-based session with modern standards.

whyNot.B: A CRL only lists revoked certificates and does not establish a secure session on the server.
whyNot.D: The requirement is to use the organization's own PKI, so a public CA certificate is not needed.
whyNot.E: A host header selects among sites on a server and provides no encryption or certificate security.

cards.front:
A manager wants to distribute a report to several other managers within the company. Some of them reside in remote locations that are not connected to the domain but have a local server. Because there is sensitive data within the report and the size of the report is beyond the limit of the email attachment size, emailing the report is not an option. Which of the following protocols should be implemented to distribute the report securely? (Select three.)
A. S/MIME
B. SSH
C. SNMPv3
D. FTPS
E. SRTP
F. HTTPS
G. LDAPS
cards.back:
B. SSH
D. FTPS
F. HTTPS
cards.why: SSH (SFTP/SCP), FTPS, and HTTPS all provide encrypted file transfer suited to moving a large sensitive report to remote servers.

whyNot.A: S/MIME secures email messages, and email is ruled out here.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 is for secure network device management, not file distribution.
whyNot.E: SRTP secures real-time voice and video media streams, not file transfers.
whyNot.G: LDAPS secures directory queries and is not a file distribution protocol.

cards.front:
An auditor is reviewing the following output from a password-cracking tool: Which of the following methods did the auditor MOST likely use?
A. Hybrid
B. Dictionary
C. Brute force
D. Rainbow table
cards.why: The tool output is not shown, so this cannot be verified; a hybrid attack combines dictionary words with appended characters or numbers, which the key indicates the output showed.

whyNot.B: A pure dictionary attack tries only listed words without modifications.
whyNot.C: Brute force tries every character combination and would not show word-based patterns.
whyNot.D: A rainbow table uses precomputed hash lookups rather than live guessing.

cards.front:
Which of the following must be intact for evidence to be admissible in court?
A. Chain of custody
B. Order of volatility
C. Legal hold
D. Preservation
cards.why: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when, proving integrity and making it admissible in court.

whyNot.B: Order of volatility dictates the sequence of collecting evidence, not its admissibility.
whyNot.C: A legal hold requires preserving relevant data but does not prove integrity of handling.
whyNot.D: Preservation protects data from change, but chain of custody is what demonstrates the evidence stayed intact.

cards.front:
A vulnerability scanner that uses its running service's access level to better assess vulnerabilities across multiple assets within an organization is performing a:
A. Credentialed scan.
B. Non-intrusive scan.
C. Privilege escalation test.
D. Passive scan.
cards.why: A credentialed scan uses authenticated access on the target to see configurations and patch levels, producing deeper and more accurate vulnerability results.

whyNot.B: A non-intrusive scan avoids disrupting systems and says nothing about access level.
whyNot.C: A privilege escalation test tries to gain higher rights rather than using given credentials.
whyNot.D: A passive scan observes traffic without probing hosts and does not use service access.

cards.front:
Which of the following cryptography algorithms will produce a fixed-length, irreversible output?
A. AES
B. 3DES
C. RSA
D. MD5
cards.why: MD5 is a hashing algorithm that produces a fixed-length 128-bit digest that cannot feasibly be reversed.

whyNot.A: AES is a symmetric cipher whose output is reversible with the key and varies with input length.
whyNot.B: 3DES is a symmetric cipher and its output is decryptable.
whyNot.C: RSA is an asymmetric cipher whose output can be decrypted with the private key.

cards.front:
A technician suspects that a system has been compromised. The technician reviews the following log entry: WARNING- hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\user32.dll WARNING- hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\kernel32.dll Based solely ono the above information, which of the following types of malware is MOST likely installed on the system?
A. Rootkit
B. Ransomware
C. Trojan
D. Backdoor
cards.why: Hash mismatches on core system DLLs indicate they were modified to hide malicious activity, which is characteristic of a rootkit.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts user files and would not typically alter core system DLLs.
whyNot.C: A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software but does not by itself imply tampered system libraries.
whyNot.D: A backdoor provides remote access but is not indicated by modified system files alone.

cards.front:
A new firewall has been places into service at an organization. However, a configuration has not been entered on the firewall. Employees on the network segment covered by the new firewall report they are unable to access the network. Which of the following steps should be completed to BEST resolve the issue?
A. The firewall should be configured to prevent user traffic form matching the implicit deny rule.
B. The firewall should be configured with access lists to allow inbound and outbound traffic.
C. The firewall should be configured with port security to allow traffic.
D. The firewall should be configured to include an explicit deny rule.
cards.back: A. The firewall should be configured to prevent user traffic form matching the implicit deny rule.
cards.why: A firewall with no configuration applies its implicit deny rule, so traffic must be explicitly permitted so it no longer matches that rule.

whyNot.B: This is the more practical remedy, since access lists permitting traffic are how you prevent the implicit deny from matching.
whyNot.C: Port security is a switch feature controlling MAC addresses and is not a firewall remedy.
whyNot.D: An explicit deny would continue blocking traffic rather than restoring access.

cards.keyDoubt: B. Configuring access lists to allow the needed inbound and outbound traffic is the concrete fix, while A is just a vague restatement of the goal.

cards.front:
A security analyst is testing both Windows and Linux systems for unauthorized DNS zone transfers within a LAN on comptia.org from example.org. Which of the following commands should the security analyst use? (Select two.)
A. 
B. 
C. dig -axfr comptia.org @example.org
D. ipconfig /flushDNS
E. 
F. dig @example.org comptia.org
cards.why: The command dig with the axfr option requests a full zone transfer for comptia.org from the server example.org, testing for unauthorized transfers.

whyNot.A: The option text is blank, so it cannot be a valid answer.
whyNot.B: The option text is blank, so it cannot be a valid answer.
whyNot.D: ipconfig /flushDNS only clears the local resolver cache and does not test zone transfers.
whyNot.E: The option text is blank, so it cannot be a valid answer.
whyNot.F: This dig query performs a normal record lookup, not a zone transfer.

cards.front:
Which of the following are the MAIN reasons why a systems administrator would install security patches in a staging environment before the patches are applied to the production server? (Select two.)
A. To prevent server availability issues
B. To verify the appropriate patch is being installed
C. To generate a new baseline hash after patching
D. To allow users to test functionality
E. To ensure users are trained on new functionality
cards.back:
A. To prevent server availability issues
D. To allow users to test functionality
cards.why: Testing patches in staging prevents outages from faulty updates and lets users validate that functionality still works before production deployment.

whyNot.B: Verifying the correct patch is a download and hash-check task, not a reason for staging.
whyNot.C: A new baseline hash is generated after patching production, not as a reason for staging.
whyNot.E: Training users on new functionality is not a goal of security patching in staging.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) drafts an agreement between the organization and its employees. The agreement outlines ramifications for releasing information without consent and/or approvals. Which of the following BEST describes this type of agreement?
A. ISA
B. NDA
C. MOU
D. SLA
cards.why: A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) legally binds employees not to release confidential information and states consequences for violations.

whyNot.A: An ISA defines the security requirements for connecting two systems between organizations.
whyNot.C: An MOU is a general statement of intent between parties and lacks specific confidentiality penalties.
whyNot.D: An SLA defines service levels expected from a provider, not information disclosure rules.

cards.front:
Which of the following would meet the requirements for multifactor authentication?
A. Username, PIN, and employee ID number
B. Fingerprint and password
C. Smart card and hardware token
D. Voice recognition and retina scan
cards.why: Fingerprint (something you are) combined with a password (something you know) uses two different factor categories, satisfying multifactor authentication.

whyNot.A: Username, PIN, and employee ID are all something you know, so this is a single factor.
whyNot.C: A smart card and hardware token are both something you have, so this is a single factor.
whyNot.D: Voice recognition and retina scan are both biometrics (something you are), so this is a single factor.

cards.front:
A manager suspects that an IT employee with elevated database access may be knowingly modifying financial transactions for the benefit of a competitor. Which of the following practices should the manager implement to validate the concern?
A. Separation of duties
B. Mandatory vacations
C. Background checks
D. Security awareness training
cards.why: Separation of duties splits critical tasks among people so no single employee can alter financial records unchecked, which limits this kind of insider fraud.

whyNot.B: Mandatory vacations make a replacement review the employee's work, which is the usual way to detect this fraud (see keyDoubt).
whyNot.C: Background checks screen people at hiring and do not validate a current suspicion.
whyNot.D: Awareness training teaches policy and does not detect deliberate, malicious tampering.

cards.keyDoubt: B, because mandatory vacations are the detective control that lets another person uncover ongoing fraud, while separation of duties is preventive.

cards.front:
A penetration tester finds that a company's login credentials for the email client were being sent in clear text. Which of the following should be done to provide encrypted logins to the email server?
A. Enable IPSec and configure SMTP.
B. Enable SSH and LDAP credentials.
C. Enable MIME services and POP3.
D. Enable an SSL certificate for IMAP services.
cards.back: D. Enable an SSL certificate for IMAP services.
cards.why: Enabling SSL/TLS on IMAP (IMAPS) encrypts the mailbox session, so credentials are no longer sent in clear text to the email server.

whyNot.A: IPSec with SMTP only covers sending mail and is not the standard way to protect client logins.
whyNot.B: SSH and LDAP credentials do not secure an email client's login to a mail server.
whyNot.C: MIME formats message content and POP3 by itself sends credentials in clear text.

cards.front:
Before an infection was detected, several of the infected devices attempted to access a URL that was similar to the company name but with two letters transposed. Which of the following BEST describes the attack vector used to infect the devices?
A. Cross-site scripting
B. DNS poisoning
C. Typo squatting
D. URL hijacking
cards.why: Typosquatting registers a domain that is a misspelling or transposition of a legitimate name, hoping users mistype it and land on a malicious site.

whyNot.A: Cross-site scripting injects script into a vulnerable site and does not rely on lookalike domains.
whyNot.B: DNS poisoning corrupts resolver records, so users would be redirected even when typing the correct name.
whyNot.D: URL hijacking is a synonym for typosquatting, but the question asks for the best-fitting specific term.

cards.front:
A system administrator is reviewing the following information from a compromised server. Given the above information, which of the following processes was MOST likely exploited via remote buffer overflow attack?
A. Apache
B. LSASS
C. MySQL
D. TFTP
cards.why: Per the key, the exhibit shows the Apache web service as the process exposed to the network and crashing or spawning shells, the pattern of a remote buffer overflow. The exhibit was not included, so this is not verified.

whyNot.B: LSASS is a Windows authentication process and is attacked differently from a network-facing web service.
whyNot.C: MySQL is a database service normally not exposed directly, so it is less likely the exploited process.
whyNot.D: TFTP is a simple file transfer service and is not the process indicated by the key.

cards.front:
Joe, a security administrator, needs to extend the organization's remote access functionality to be used by staff while travelling. Joe needs to maintain separate access control functionalities for internal, external, and VOIP services. Which of the following represents the BEST access technology for Joe to use?
A. RADIUS
B. TACACS+
C. Diameter
D. Kerberos
cards.why: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, so Joe can apply distinct access control policies for internal, external, and VOIP services.

whyNot.A: RADIUS combines authentication and authorization, so it cannot separate access control functions as granularly.
whyNot.C: Diameter is a RADIUS successor mainly used in carrier and mobile networks and does not fit this need.
whyNot.D: Kerberos provides ticket-based single sign-on and is not a remote access AAA service with separated functions.

cards.front:
The availability of a system has been labeled as the highest priority. Which of the following should be focused on the MOST to ensure the objective?
A. Authentication
B. HVAC
C. Full-disk encryption
D. File integrity checking
cards.why: HVAC keeps equipment within safe temperature and humidity, preventing hardware failure and downtime, which directly supports the availability goal.

whyNot.A: Authentication supports confidentiality by controlling who gets in and does not keep systems running.
whyNot.C: Full-disk encryption protects confidentiality and can add overhead without improving uptime.
whyNot.D: File integrity checking detects unauthorized changes and supports integrity, not availability.

cards.front:
As part of the SDLC, a third party is hired to perform a penetration test. The third party will have access to the source code, integration tests, and network diagrams. Which of the following BEST describes the assessment being performed?
A. Black box
B. Regression
C. White box
D. Fuzzing
cards.why: A white box (known environment) test gives the tester full knowledge, such as source code and network diagrams, of the system being tested.

whyNot.A: Black box testing gives the tester no internal knowledge of the target.
whyNot.B: Regression testing re-checks that changes did not break existing functionality and is not a penetration test type.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing sends malformed input to find flaws and does not describe the level of access given.

cards.front:
A dumpster diver recovers several hard drives from a company and is able to obtain confidential data from one of the hard drives. The company then discovers its information is posted online. Which of the following methods would have MOST likely prevented the data from being exposed?
A. Removing the hard drive from its enclosure
B. Using software to repeatedly rewrite over the disk space
C. Using Blowfish encryption on the hard drives
D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.back: D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.why: Degaussing with strong magnetic fields destroys the magnetic data on a hard drive, so recovered drives would have been unreadable.

whyNot.A: Removing the drive from its enclosure leaves all the data intact and readable.
whyNot.B: Overwriting can sanitize a drive, but it is slower and can miss bad sectors, so degaussing is the stronger choice here.
whyNot.C: Blowfish encryption would protect data only if implemented and keyed properly, and the question asks about data destruction.

cards.front:
Which of the following are methods to implement HA in a web application server environment? (Select two.)
A. Load balancers
B. Application layer firewalls
C. Reverse proxies
D. VPN concentrators
E. Routers
cards.back:
A. Load balancers
B. Application layer firewalls
cards.why: Load balancers distribute requests across multiple web servers and route around failed nodes, providing high availability. Application layer firewalls filter traffic and do not add redundancy.

whyNot.C: Reverse proxies can front and balance multiple servers, so they are a valid HA method (see keyDoubt).
whyNot.D: VPN concentrators terminate remote access tunnels and do not provide web server redundancy.
whyNot.E: Routers forward packets and do not provide server-level failover for a web application.

cards.keyDoubt: C instead of B, because reverse proxies can balance and fail over web servers, while application layer firewalls are a security control, not an HA method.

cards.front:
An application developer is designing an application involving secure transports from one service to another that will pass over port 80 for a request. Which of the following secure protocols is the developer MOST likely to use?
A. FTPS
B. SFTP
C. SSL
D. LDAPS
E. SSH
cards.why: SSL/TLS can secure application traffic between services, and the key treats it as the secure transport wrapped around a request on port 80.

whyNot.A: FTPS secures file transfers over FTP and uses FTP ports, not a web request on port 80.
whyNot.B: SFTP runs over SSH for file transfer and uses port 22.
whyNot.D: LDAPS secures directory queries and uses port 636.
whyNot.E: SSH provides secure remote shells and tunnels on port 22 and is not the transport for a port 80 request.

cards.front:
Which of the following precautions MINIMIZES the risk from network attacks directed at multifunction printers, as well as the impact on functionality at the same time?
A. Isolating the systems using VLANs
B. Installing a software-based IPS on all devices
C. Enabling full disk encryption
D. Implementing a unique user PIN access functions
cards.back: A. Isolating the systems using VLANs
cards.why: Placing printers on their own VLAN segments network attacks away from other systems while leaving printing fully functional for users.

whyNot.B: Printers generally cannot run host-based IPS software, so this is impractical.
whyNot.C: Full disk encryption protects stored data and does not reduce network attack exposure.
whyNot.D: User PINs control who can print and do not stop network-based attacks on the device.

cards.front:
After an identified security breach, an analyst is tasked to initiate the IR process. Which of the following is the NEXT step the analyst should take?
A. Recovery
B. Identification
C. Preparation
D. Documentation
E. Escalation
cards.why: Identification confirms and scopes the incident, determining what occurred and its extent, and it begins the active IR process before containment.

whyNot.A: Recovery comes near the end, after containment and eradication.
whyNot.C: Preparation happens before any incident occurs.
whyNot.D: Documentation continues throughout the process and is not the next distinct phase.
whyNot.E: Escalation follows once the incident is validated and scoped, so it comes after identification.

cards.front:
A company was recently audited by a third party. The audit revealed the company's network devices were transferring files in the clear. Which of the following protocols should the company use to transfer files?
A. HTTPS
B. LDAPS
C. SCP
D. SNMPv3
cards.why: SCP transfers files over SSH, encrypting both the credentials and the data in transit and replacing clear text transfer protocols such as FTP or TFTP.

whyNot.A: HTTPS encrypts web traffic and is not the usual file transfer method for network devices.
whyNot.B: LDAPS secures directory service queries and is not a file transfer protocol.
whyNot.D: SNMPv3 secures device management and monitoring and does not transfer files.

cards.front:
During a monthly vulnerability scan, a server was flagged for being vulnerable to an Apache Struts exploit. Upon further investigation, the developer responsible for the server informs the security team that Apache Struts is not installed on the server. Which of the following BEST describes how the security team should reach to this incident?
A. The finding is a false positive and can be disregarded
B. The Struts module needs to be hardened on the server
C. The Apache software on the server needs to be patched and updated
D. The server has been compromised by malware and needs to be quarantined.
cards.back: A. The finding is a false positive and can be disregarded
cards.why: The scanner reported a vulnerability for software that is not installed, which is a false positive and needs no remediation after the developer confirms it.

whyNot.B: You cannot harden a Struts module that is not installed.
whyNot.C: Patching Apache would not address a flaw in Struts, which is a separate framework.
whyNot.D: Nothing indicates compromise, as the only evidence is a scanner finding for absent software.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to protect data stored on mobile devices that are used to scan and record assets in a warehouse. The control must automatically destroy the secure container of mobile devices if they leave the warehouse. Which of the following should the administrator implement? (Select two.)
A. Geofencing
B. Remote wipe
C. Near-field communication
D. Push notification services
E. Containerization
cards.why: Geofencing triggers an action when a device leaves a defined area, and containerization keeps data in a secure container that can be destroyed on that trigger.

whyNot.B: Remote wipe erases the whole device and the question asks to destroy only the secure container automatically.
whyNot.C: NFC is short-range communication and does not detect location or destroy data.
whyNot.D: Push notifications deliver messages to the device and do not enforce location-based controls.

cards.front:
A security analyst is performing a quantitative risk analysis. The risk analysis should show the potential monetary loss each time a threat or event occurs. Given this requirement, which of the following concepts would assist the analyst in determining this value? (Select two.)
A. ALE
B. AV
C. ARO
D. EF
E. ROI
cards.why: ALE annualizes loss as SLE times ARO, so these two are annual-frequency concepts, not the per-occurrence loss the question asks for.

whyNot.B: AV is an input to SLE (AV x EF) but is not itself the loss per event.
whyNot.D: EF is the percentage of asset value lost per event, a component of SLE.
whyNot.E: ROI measures the financial return on a security investment, not loss from a threat event.

cards.keyDoubt: B and D: SLE = AV x EF gives the monetary loss per occurrence, while ALE and ARO are annualized figures.

cards.front:
Which of the following AES modes of operation provide authentication? (Select two.)
A. CCM
B. CBC
C. GCM
D. DSA
E. CFB
cards.why: CCM and GCM are authenticated-encryption (AEAD) modes that provide both confidentiality and integrity or authentication of the data.

whyNot.B: CBC provides confidentiality only and has no built-in authentication tag.
whyNot.D: DSA is a digital signature algorithm, not an AES mode of operation.
whyNot.E: CFB is a stream-like confidentiality mode with no authentication.

cards.front:
An audit takes place after company-wide restricting, in which several employees changed roles. The following deficiencies are found during the audit regarding access to confidential data: Which of the following would be the BEST method to prevent similar audit findings in the future?
A. Implement separation of duties for the payroll department.
B. Implement a DLP solution on the payroll and human resources servers.
C. Implement rule-based access controls on the human resources server.
D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews.
cards.back: D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews.
cards.why: Regular permission auditing and reviews (user access recertification) catch stale privileges left behind when employees change roles.

whyNot.A: Separation of duties splits tasks between people but does not remove outdated permissions after role changes.
whyNot.B: DLP monitors data leaving the network and does not fix excessive access rights.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control enforces static rules but does not detect privilege creep from role changes.

cards.front:
