cards.why: AES-256 is a strong, widely approved symmetric cipher that is efficient on mobile devices and suitable for protecting data on phones.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is asymmetric and used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk device encryption.
whyNot.B: A one-time pad is impractical for device storage because it needs a truly random key as long as the data.
whyNot.C: 3DES is a legacy cipher with a small block size and is deprecated.

cards.front:
An organization relies heavily on an application that has a high frequency of security updates. At present, the security team only updates the application on the first Monday of each month, even though the security updates are released as often as twice a week. Which of the following would be the BEST method of updating this application?
A. Configure testing and automate patch management for the application.
B. Configure security control testing for the application.
C. Manually apply updates for the application when they are released.
D. Configure a sandbox for testing patches before the scheduled monthly update.
cards.back: A. Configure testing and automate patch management for the application.
cards.why: Automating patch management with testing lets frequent security updates be validated and deployed quickly, closing the exposure window of a monthly schedule.

whyNot.B: Security control testing checks controls but does not address deploying frequent patches.
whyNot.C: Manual updates on release are error-prone and untested, and do not scale to twice-weekly releases.
whyNot.D: A sandbox helps test but still ties deployment to the slow monthly schedule.

cards.front:
A technician must configure a firewall to block external DNS traffic from entering a network. Which of the following ports should they block on the firewall?
A. 53
B. 110
C. 143
D. 443
cards.why: DNS uses port 53, so blocking port 53 on the firewall stops external DNS traffic.

whyNot.B: Port 110 is POP3 for email retrieval.
whyNot.C: Port 143 is IMAP for email retrieval.
whyNot.D: Port 443 is HTTPS for secure web traffic.

cards.front:
A software development company needs to share information between two remote servers, using encryption to protect it. A programmer suggests developing a new encryption protocol, arguing that using an unknown protocol with secure, existing cryptographic algorithm libraries will provide strong encryption without being susceptible to attacks on other known protocols. Which of the following summarizes the BEST response to the programmer's proposal?
A. The newly developed protocol will only be as secure as the underlying cryptographic algorithms used.
B. New protocols often introduce unexpected vulnerabilities, even when developed with otherwise secure and tested algorithm libraries.
C. A programmer should have specialized training in protocol development before attempting to design a new encryption protocol.
D. The obscurity value of unproven protocols against attacks often outweighs the potential for introducing new vulnerabilities.
cards.back: B. New protocols often introduce unexpected vulnerabilities, even when developed with otherwise secure and tested algorithm libraries.
cards.why: Custom protocols are prone to design flaws even when built on sound algorithms, so well-vetted existing protocols are preferred over new unproven ones.

whyNot.A: Protocol security depends on its design too, not only on the underlying algorithms.
whyNot.C: Training helps but does not address why unproven protocols are risky.
whyNot.D: Security through obscurity is unreliable and does not outweigh the risk of new vulnerabilities.

cards.front:
A security technician would like to obscure sensitive data within a file so that it can be transferred without causing suspicion. Which of the following technologies would BEST be suited to accomplish this?
A. Transport Encryption
B. Stream Encryption
C. Digital Signature
D. Steganography
cards.back:
D. Steganography

Steganography is the process of hiding a message in another message so as to obfuscate its importance. It is also the process of hiding a message in a medium such as a digital image, audio file, or other file.
cards.why: Steganography hides data inside another file such as an image, so the transfer does not look suspicious.

whyNot.A: Transport encryption protects data in transit but the encrypted traffic is plainly visible as such.
whyNot.B: Stream encryption scrambles data but does not conceal that secret data exists.
whyNot.C: A digital signature provides authenticity and integrity, not concealment.

cards.front:
A supervisor in your organization was demoted on Friday afternoon. The supervisor had the ability to modify the contents of a confidential database, as well as other managerial permissions. On Monday morning, the database administrator reported that log files indicated that several records were missing from the database. Which of the following risk mitigation strategies should have been implemented when the supervisor was demoted?
A. Incident management
B. Routine auditing
C. IT governance
D. Monthly user rights reviews
cards.why: Routine auditing of logs and permissions would have detected the demoted supervisor's retained access and unauthorized changes, so it would have been the control to catch the problem.

whyNot.A: Incident management responds after an incident and would not prevent retained access.
whyNot.C: IT governance is a broad framework, not a specific control for this issue.
whyNot.D: Monthly rights reviews are too infrequent to have caught a change made over one weekend.

cards.keyDoubt: D. User rights and permissions reviews, performed when a role changes, are the control that would have removed the supervisor's access, whereas auditing only detects misuse afterward.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types is being carried out where a target is being sent unsolicited messages via Bluetooth?
A. War chalking
B. Bluejacking
C. Bluesnarfing
D. Rogue tethering
cards.back:
B. Bluejacking

Bluejacking is the sending of unsolicited messages over Bluetooth to Bluetooth-enabled devices such as mobile phones, PDAs or laptop computers, sending a vCard which typically contains a message in the name field (i.e., for bluedating or bluechat) to another B...
cards.why: Bluejacking is sending unsolicited messages to Bluetooth-enabled devices.

whyNot.A: War chalking marks the locations of open wireless networks.
whyNot.C: Bluesnarfing steals data from a Bluetooth device rather than sending messages.
whyNot.D: Rogue tethering is creating an unauthorized network connection through a mobile device.

cards.front:
Joe is exchanging encrypted email with another party. Joe encrypts the initial email with a key. When Joe receives a response, he is unable to decrypt the response with the same key he used initially. Which of the following would explain the situation?
A. An ephemeral key was used for one of the messages
B. A stream cipher was used for the initial email; a block cipher was used for the reply
C. Out-of-band key exchange has taken place
D. Asymmetric encryption is being used
cards.back:
D. Asymmetric encryption is being used

Asymmetric algorithms use two keys to encrypt and decrypt data. These asymmetric keys are referred to as the public key and the private key.
cards.why: With asymmetric encryption, the sender encrypts with the recipient's public key, and the reply is encrypted with a different key, so the same key cannot decrypt it.

whyNot.A: An ephemeral key is possible but does not best explain why the reply needs a different key.
whyNot.B: Cipher type does not change that a symmetric key would work in both directions.
whyNot.C: Out-of-band key exchange only shares keys and would not prevent decrypting with the same key.

cards.front:
Recently several employees were victims of a phishing email that appeared to originate from the company president. The email claimed the employees would be disciplined if they did not click on a malicious link in the message. Which of the following principles of social engineering made this attack successful?
A. Authority
B. Spamming
C. Social proof
D. Scarcity
cards.why: The attacker impersonated the company president, exploiting the Authority principle: employees comply with instructions from a figure of power, especially when discipline is threatened.

whyNot.B: Spamming is a delivery method for unsolicited mail, not a social engineering principle.
whyNot.C: Social proof relies on people copying what others are doing, which is not present here.
whyNot.D: Scarcity pressures victims with limited availability or time, not with a superior's threat of discipline.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the LEAST secure hashing algorithm?
A. SHA1
B. RIPEMD
C. MD5
D. DES
cards.why: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest and has well-known practical collision attacks, making it the weakest of the listed hashing algorithms.

whyNot.A: SHA1 is deprecated because of collision attacks, but it has a longer 160-bit digest and is harder to attack than MD5.
whyNot.B: RIPEMD is a hash family with no practical breaks in its stronger variants, so it is more secure than MD5.
whyNot.D: DES is a symmetric encryption cipher, not a hashing algorithm, so it does not fit the question.

cards.front:
An employee uses RDP to connect back to the office network. If RDP is misconfigured, which of the following security exposures would this lead to?
A. A virus on the administrator's desktop would be able to sniff the administrator's username and password.
B. Result in an attacker being able to phish the employee's username and password.
C. A social engineering attack could occur, resulting in the employee's password being extracted.
D. A man in the middle attack could occur, resulting the employee's username and password being captured.
cards.back: D. A man in the middle attack could occur, resulting the employee's username and password being captured.
cards.why: A misconfigured RDP session may lack proper encryption or server authentication, allowing a man-in-the-middle attacker to intercept and capture credentials.

whyNot.A: A virus on the administrator's desktop is a host compromise unrelated to how RDP is configured.
whyNot.B: Phishing is an email or web lure that does not depend on RDP configuration.
whyNot.C: Social engineering targets people, not protocol settings, so RDP misconfiguration is not the cause.

cards.front:
Joe, the security administrator, sees this in a vulnerability scan report: "The server 10.1.2.232 is running Apache 2.2.20 which may be vulnerable to a mod_cgi exploit." Joe verifies that the mod_cgi module is not enabled on 10.1.2.232. This message is an example of:
A. a threat.
B. a risk.
C. a false negative.
D. a false positive.
cards.why: The scanner flagged a vulnerability that does not exist because the mod_cgi module is disabled, which is a false positive.

whyNot.A: A threat is a potential source of harm, not an erroneous scan finding.
whyNot.B: Risk is the likelihood and impact of exploitation, and here the flagged vulnerability is not present.
whyNot.C: A false negative would be a real vulnerability the scanner failed to report, the opposite of this case.

cards.front:
An auditor has identified an access control system that can incorrectly accept an access attempt from an unauthorized user. Which of the following authentication systems has the auditor reviewed?
A. Password-based
B. Biometric-based
C. Location-based
D. Certificate-based
cards.why: Biometric systems have a false acceptance rate, meaning they can wrongly admit an unauthorized user whose features resemble an enrolled one.

whyNot.A: Passwords either match exactly or do not, so there is no probabilistic false acceptance.
whyNot.C: Location-based checks use deterministic criteria such as IP address or GPS rather than fuzzy matching.
whyNot.D: Certificate validation is cryptographic and exact, so it does not incorrectly accept near matches.

cards.front:
The Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of a company, Ann, is putting together a hardware budget for the next 10 years. She is asking for the average lifespan of each hardware device so that she is able to calculate when she will have to replace each device. Which of the following categories BEST describes what she is looking for?
A. ALE
B. MTTR
C. MTBF
D. MTTF
cards.why: MTTF (mean time to failure) is the expected lifespan of a non-repairable device, which is what she needs to schedule replacements.

whyNot.A: ALE is annualized loss expectancy, a financial risk figure rather than a device lifespan.
whyNot.B: MTTR is the mean time to repair, how long fixing a failure takes.
whyNot.C: MTBF measures average time between failures of repairable systems, not the end of a device's life.

cards.front:
A software developer wants to ensure that the application is verifying that a key is valid before establishing SSL connections with random remote hosts on the Internet. Which of the following should be used in the code? (Select TWO.)
A. Escrowed keys
B. SSL symmetric encryption key
C. Software code private key
D. Remote server public key
E. OCSP
cards.back:
C. Software code private key
E. OCSP
cards.why: OCSP lets the code check in real time whether a certificate or key has been revoked, which is the validity check the developer wants.

whyNot.A: Escrowed keys are stored with a third party for recovery and do not validate remote hosts.
whyNot.B: A symmetric session key is created after trust is established and cannot verify a remote key.
whyNot.D: The remote server's public key is actually needed to validate the host's certificate, so this option is arguably correct despite not being keyed.

cards.keyDoubt: D, not C: the code validates the remote server's public key and certificate, while its own private key is unrelated to verifying remote hosts.

cards.front:
A security guard has informed the Chief Information Security Officer that a person with a tablet has been walking around the building. The guard also noticed strange white markings in different areas of the parking lot. The person is attempting which of the following types of attacks?
A. Jamming
B. War chalking
C. Packet sniffing
D. Near field communication
cards.why: War chalking is marking public spaces with symbols to advertise open wireless networks, matching the white markings and the person walking around with a tablet.

whyNot.A: Jamming disrupts wireless signals and involves no chalk markings.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures traffic and leaves no physical markings in a parking lot.
whyNot.D: NFC attacks need very close proximity and do not involve marking locations.

cards.front:
A system administrator is configuring a site-to-site VPN tunnel. Which of the following should be configured on the VPN concentrator during the IKE phase?
A. RIPEMD
B. ECDHE
C. Diffie-Hellman
D. HTTPS
cards.why: During IKE, the VPN peers use Diffie-Hellman key exchange to securely establish shared keying material for the tunnel.

whyNot.A: RIPEMD is a hash function and does not perform the IKE key exchange.
whyNot.B: ECDHE is an ephemeral key exchange used mainly in TLS, whereas IKE is classically configured with Diffie-Hellman groups.
whyNot.D: HTTPS is a web protocol and is not part of IKE negotiation.

cards.front:
A network operations manager has added a second row of server racks in the datacenter. These racks face the opposite direction of the first row of racks. Which of the following is the reason the manager installed the racks this way?
A. To lower energy consumption by sharing power outlets
B. To create environmental hot and cold isles
C. To eliminate the potential for electromagnetic interference
D. To maximize fire suppression capabilities
cards.back: B. To create environmental hot and cold isles
cards.why: Racks facing opposite directions create alternating hot and cold aisles, improving cooling efficiency by separating intake and exhaust airflow.

whyNot.A: Rack orientation does not let racks share power outlets or reduce energy that way.
whyNot.C: EMI is reduced by shielding and distance, not by rack direction.
whyNot.D: Fire suppression depends on the system design and not on which way racks face.

cards.front:
Phishing emails frequently take advantage of high-profile catastrophes reported in the news. Which of the following principles BEST describes the weakness being exploited?
A. Intimidation
B. Scarcity
C. Authority
D. Social proof
cards.why: Social proof exploits people's tendency to follow what others are doing or reacting to, and attackers use widely reported disasters to make fraudulent requests seem legitimate.

whyNot.A: Intimidation uses threats or fear of consequences, which the scenario does not describe.
whyNot.B: Scarcity relies on limited supply or time pressure rather than on news events.
whyNot.C: Authority depends on impersonating a trusted figure, which is not described.

cards.front:
New magnetic locks were ordered for an entire building. In accordance with company policy, employee safety is the top priority. In case of a fire where electricity is cut, which of the following should be taken into consideration when installing the new locks?
A. Fail safe
B. Fault tolerance
C. Fail secure
D. Redundancy
cards.why: A fail-safe lock unlocks when power is lost, so people can exit during a fire, which puts human safety first.

whyNot.B: Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep running through component failure, not a lock failure mode.
whyNot.C: Fail secure keeps doors locked when power is lost, which could trap occupants during a fire.
whyNot.D: Redundancy adds backup components and does not define how a lock behaves without power.

cards.front:
Anne, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), has reported that she is getting multiple telephone calls from someone claiming to be from the helpdesk. The caller is asking to verify her network authentication credentials because her computer is broadcasting across the network. This is MOST likely which of the following types of attacks?
A. Vishing
B. Impersonation
C. Spim
D. Scareware
cards.why: Vishing is social engineering by voice or phone, and here the caller poses as the helpdesk to extract credentials.

whyNot.B: Impersonation is a general tactic used in the call, but the specific attack type here is vishing.
whyNot.C: Spim is spam sent through instant messaging, not telephone calls.
whyNot.D: Scareware uses fake alerts to push software installs, rather than a call asking for credentials.

cards.front:
An administrator discovers the following log entry on a server: Nov 12 2013 00:23:45 httpd[2342]: GET /app2/prod/proc/process.php?input=change;cd%20../../../etc;cat%20shadow Which of the following attacks is being attempted?
A. Command injection
B. Password attack
C. Buffer overflow
D. Cross-site scripting
cards.why: The input parameter appends shell commands (cd, cat shadow) after a semicolon, which is command injection aimed at reading the system's password hashes.

whyNot.B: A password attack would involve guessing or cracking credentials, not injecting shell commands.
whyNot.C: A buffer overflow sends oversized input to corrupt memory, not shell metacharacters.
whyNot.D: Cross-site scripting injects client-side script into pages and does not run server commands.

cards.front:
A security team wants to establish an Incident Response plan. The team has never experienced an incident. Which of the following would BEST help them establish plans and procedures?
A. Table top exercises
B. Lessons learned
C. Escalation procedures
D. Recovery procedures
cards.why: Tabletop exercises let a team walk through simulated incident scenarios to develop and test response plans without needing real incident experience.

whyNot.B: Lessons learned come from reviewing a real incident, which this team has never had.
whyNot.C: Escalation procedures are one component of a plan, not a way to build the plan.
whyNot.D: Recovery procedures are one part of the plan and cannot be established without first scenario-testing the response.

cards.front:
Which of the following would verify that a threat does exist and security controls can easily be bypassed without actively testing an application?
A. Protocol analyzer
B. Vulnerability scan
C. Penetration test
D. Port scanner
cards.back:
B. Vulnerability scan

A vulnerability scan is the automated process of proactively identifying security vulnerabilities of computing systems in a network in order to determine if and where a system can be exploited and/or threatened.
cards.why: A vulnerability scan passively identifies weaknesses and missing controls, showing that a threat exists without exploiting the application.

whyNot.A: A protocol analyzer captures and inspects traffic but does not identify vulnerabilities or weak controls.
whyNot.C: A penetration test actively exploits weaknesses, which the question rules out.
whyNot.D: A port scanner only finds open ports and services, not whether controls can be bypassed.

cards.front:
Which of the following technologies would be MOST appropriate to utilize when testing a new software patch before a company-wide deployment?
A. Cloud computing
B. Virtualization
C. Redundancy
D. Application control
cards.back:
B. Virtualization

Virtualization is used to host one or more operating systems in the memory of a single host computer and allows multiple operating systems to run simultaneously on the same hardware, reducing costs.
cards.why: Virtualization lets the company test the patch in an isolated VM or snapshot that can be reverted, without risking production systems.

whyNot.A: Cloud computing is a hosting model and does not itself provide an isolated, revertible test environment.
whyNot.C: Redundancy provides availability through duplicate components and has nothing to do with patch testing.
whyNot.D: Application control restricts which software can run and does not validate patches.

cards.front:
A system administrator needs to implement 802.1x whereby when a user logs into the network, the authentication server communicates to the network switch and assigns the user to the proper VLAN. Which of the following protocols should be used?
A. RADIUS
B. Kerberos
C. LDAP
D. MSCHAP
cards.why: RADIUS is the AAA protocol used in 802.1X to authenticate users and return attributes such as VLAN assignment to the switch.

whyNot.B: Kerberos issues tickets for service authentication and does not return VLAN attributes to a switch.
whyNot.C: LDAP is a directory access protocol and does not instruct switches to place users in VLANs.
whyNot.D: MSCHAP is an authentication method that RADIUS can carry, not the protocol that assigns VLANs.

cards.front:
A security administrator receives notice that a third-party certificate authority has been compromised, and new certificates will need to be issued. Which of the following should the administrator submit to receive a new certificate?
A. CRL
B. OSCP
C. PFX
D. CSR
E. CA
cards.why: A Certificate Signing Request (CSR) is submitted to a certificate authority to request a new signed certificate.

whyNot.A: A CRL lists revoked certificates and is not used to request new ones.
whyNot.B: OCSP checks the revocation status of a certificate and does not request issuance.
whyNot.C: PFX is a file format for bundling certificates and private keys, not a request.
whyNot.E: The CA is the entity that issues the certificate, not what you submit to it.

cards.front:
A company wants to host a publicly available server that performs the following functions: Evaluates MX record lookup Can perform authenticated requests for A and AAA records Uses RRSIG Which of the following should the company use to fulfill the above requirements?
A. DNSSEC
B. SFTP
C. nslookup
D. dig
E. LDAPS
cards.back:
A. DNSSEC

DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) provides, among other things, cryptographic authenticity of responses using Resource Record Signatures (RRSIG) and authenticated denial of existence using Next-Secure (NSEC) and Hashed-NSEC records (NSEC3).
cards.why: DNSSEC adds RRSIG signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify the authenticity and integrity of responses such as MX, A, and AAAA lookups.

whyNot.B: SFTP is a secure file transfer protocol and has nothing to do with DNS records.
whyNot.C: nslookup is a client query tool, not a service a company hosts.
whyNot.D: dig is a client query tool that can display RRSIG records but does not provide them.
whyNot.E: LDAPS is LDAP over TLS for directory services, not DNS.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing training for corporate users on basic security principles for personal email accounts. Which of the following should be mentioned as the MOST secure way for password recovery?
A. Utilizing a single Qfor password recovery
B. Sending a PIN to a smartphone through text message
C. Utilizing CAPTCHA to avoid brute force attacks
D. Use a different e-mail address to recover password
cards.back: B. Sending a PIN to a smartphone through text message
cards.why: Sending a PIN to a phone is out-of-band verification, which proves possession of a second channel the attacker likely does not control.

whyNot.A: A single security question relies on guessable or publicly researchable answers.
whyNot.C: CAPTCHA slows automated attacks but is not a password recovery method.
whyNot.D: A second email account may itself be weakly protected or compromised, so it adds little assurance.

cards.front:
A company researched the root cause of a recent vulnerability in its software. It was determined that the vulnerability was the result of two updates made in the last release. Each update alone would not have resulted in the vulnerability. In order to prevent similar situations in the future, the company should improve which of the following?
A. Change management procedures
B. Job rotation policies
C. Incident response management
D. Least privilege access controls
cards.why: Change management requires review, testing, and approval of combined changes, which would catch interactions between two updates before release.

whyNot.B: Job rotation reduces fraud and insider risk, not interaction flaws between software changes.
whyNot.C: Incident response handles problems after they occur and does not prevent them in the release process.
whyNot.D: Least privilege limits access rights and does not govern how code changes are reviewed.

cards.front:
A computer on a company network was infected with a zero-day exploit after an employee accidently opened an email that contained malicious content. The employee recognized the email as malicious and was attempting to delete it, but accidently opened it. Which of the following should be done to prevent this scenario from occurring again in the future?
A. Install host-based firewalls on all computers that have an email client installed
B. Set the email program default to open messages in plain text
C. Install end-point protection on all computers that access web email
D. Create new email spam filters to delete all messages from that sender
cards.back: B. Set the email program default to open messages in plain text
cards.why: Opening messages in plain text prevents scripts and active content from executing, so an accidental open of a malicious email is far less harmful.

whyNot.A: Host-based firewalls filter network traffic and do not stop malicious content rendered by the email client.
whyNot.C: Endpoint protection relies on known signatures or behavior and is weaker against zero-day exploits than disabling active content.
whyNot.D: Blocking one sender does nothing against future malicious emails from other senders.

cards.front:
A company wants to ensure that the validity of publicly trusted certificates used by its web server can be determined even during an extended internet outage. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Recovery agent
B. Ocsp
C. Crl
D. Key escrow
cards.why: A CRL can be downloaded and cached locally, so certificate validity can still be checked during an extended internet outage.

whyNot.A: A recovery agent recovers encrypted data and does not check certificate validity.
whyNot.B: OCSP queries a responder online in real time, so it fails without internet access.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores keys for recovery and does not validate certificates.

cards.keyDoubt: C. A cached CRL works offline, while OCSP requires live connectivity to the responder.

cards.front:
An administrator intends to configure an IPSec solution that provides ESP with integrity protection, but not confidentiality protection. Which of the following AES modes of operation would meet this integrity-only requirement?
A. HMAC
B. PCBC
C. CBC
D. GCM
E. CFB
cards.why: HMAC provides integrity and authentication without encrypting data, matching ESP configured for integrity only, although it is technically not an AES mode.

whyNot.B: PCBC is a block cipher mode that provides confidentiality, not integrity-only protection.
whyNot.C: CBC is an encryption mode that provides confidentiality without built-in integrity.
whyNot.D: GCM provides both encryption and authentication, so it adds confidentiality the requirement excludes.
whyNot.E: CFB is an encryption mode that provides confidentiality without integrity.

cards.front:
The chief security officer (CS0) has issued a new policy that requires that all internal websites be configured for HTTPS traffic only. The network administrator has been tasked to update all internal sites without incurring additional costs. Which of the following is the best solution for the network administrator to secure each internal website?
A. Use certificates signed by the company CA
B. Use a signing certificate as a wild card certificate
C. Use certificates signed by a public ca
D. Use a self-signed certificate on each internal server
cards.back:
A. Use certificates signed by the company CA

This is a way to update all internal sites without incurring additional costs? To be a CA (Certificate Authority), you need an infrastructure that consists of considerable operational elements, hardware, software, policy frameworks and practice statements, aud...
cards.why: An internal company CA can issue trusted certificates at no extra cost, and domain-joined clients already trust it.

whyNot.B: A signing certificate used as a wildcard breaks certificate practices and exposes the CA key.
whyNot.C: Public CA certificates generally cost money, violating the no-additional-cost requirement.
whyNot.D: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by clients, causing warnings and making management harder.

cards.front:
A security program manager wants to actively test the security posture of a system. The system is not yet in production and has no uptime requirement or active user base. Which of the following methods will produce a report which shows vulnerabilities that were actually exploited?
A. Peer review
B. Component testing
C. Penetration testing
D. Vulnerability testing
cards.back:
C. Penetration testing

A penetration test, or pen test, is an attempt to evaluate the security of an IT infrastructure by safely trying to exploit vulnerabilities.
cards.why: Penetration testing actively exploits vulnerabilities and reports which ones were actually exploited, which suits a non-production system.

whyNot.A: Peer review examines code or designs manually and does not exploit anything.
whyNot.B: Component testing checks individual parts for correct function, not exploitable vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Vulnerability testing identifies potential weaknesses but does not exploit them.

cards.front:
A new intern in the purchasing department requires read access to shared documents. Permissions are normally controlled through a group called "Purchasing", however, the purchasing group permissions allow write access. Which of the following would be the BEST course of action?
A. Modify all the shared files with read only permissions for the intern.
B. Create a new group that has only read permissions for the files.
C. Remove all permissions for the shared files.
D. Add the intern to the "Purchasing" group.
cards.back: B. Create a new group that has only read permissions for the files.
cards.why: A new read-only group follows least privilege by granting the intern only the access needed without altering existing permissions.

whyNot.A: Changing permissions on every file is labor-intensive and error-prone, and it would affect other users.
whyNot.C: Removing all permissions would deny the intern the read access required.
whyNot.D: The Purchasing group grants write access, violating least privilege.

cards.front:
A business has recently deployed laptops to all sales employees. The laptops will be used primarily from home offices and while traveling, and a high amount of wireless mobile use is expected. To protect the laptops while connected to untrusted wireless networks, which of the following would be the BEST method for reducing the risk of having the laptops compromised?
A. MAC filtering
B. Virtualization
C. OS hardening
D. Application white-listing
cards.why: OS hardening reduces the attack surface of the laptops by disabling unneeded services, applying patches, and enabling host firewalls on untrusted networks.

whyNot.A: MAC filtering is easily spoofed and is only configured on networks you control.
whyNot.B: Virtualization does not by itself protect the host OS on untrusted networks.
whyNot.D: Application whitelisting limits executable software but does not address network-based attacks on the OS.

cards.front:
During a data breach cleanup, it is discovered that not all of the sites involved have the necessary data wiping tools. The necessary tools are quickly distributed to the required technicians, but when should this problem BEST be revisited?
A. Reporting
B. Preparation
C. Mitigation
D. Lessons Learned
cards.why: The Lessons Learned phase reviews what went wrong, such as missing tools, and drives improvements to future incident response preparation.

whyNot.A: Reporting communicates incident details and does not analyze process gaps.
whyNot.B: Preparation is when the tools should have been staffed and stocked, not when the problem is best reviewed afterward.
whyNot.C: Mitigation focuses on limiting damage during the incident, not on reviewing the response afterward.

cards.front:
Joe, a technician, is working remotely with his company provided laptop at the coffee shop near his home. Joe is concerned that another patron of the coffee shop may be trying to access his laptop. Which of the following is an appropriate control to use to prevent the other patron from accessing Joe's laptop directly?
A. full-disk encryption
B. Host-based firewall
C. Current antivirus definitions
D. Latest OS updates
cards.why: A host-based firewall blocks unsolicited inbound connections to the laptop, which directly prevents another patron on the same network from reaching its services.

whyNot.A: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest if the device is stolen, not against network connections.
whyNot.C: Antivirus detects malware but does not block direct network access attempts.
whyNot.D: OS updates patch vulnerabilities but do not control which connections are allowed.

cards.front:
An attacker uses a network sniffer to capture the packets of a transaction that adds $20 to a gift card. The attacker then user a function of the sniffer to push those packets back onto the network again, adding another $20 to the gift card. This can be done many times. Which of the following describes this type of attack?
A. Integer overflow attack
B. Smurf attack
C. Replay attack
D. Buffer overflow attack
E. Cross-site scripting attack
cards.why: A replay attack captures legitimate transaction packets and retransmits them to repeat the transaction, which matches adding $20 repeatedly.

whyNot.A: Integer overflow exploits arithmetic limits in variable storage, not retransmitted captured packets.
whyNot.B: A Smurf attack floods a victim with spoofed ICMP echo replies via broadcast amplification.
whyNot.D: Buffer overflow writes excess data past a memory buffer, not resending captured traffic.
whyNot.E: Cross-site scripting injects malicious script into web pages viewed by other users.

cards.front:
An organization is moving its human resources system to a cloud services provider. The company plans to continue using internal usernames and passwords with the service provider, but the security manager does not want the service provider to have a company of the passwords. Which of the following options meets all of these requirements?
A. Two-factor authentication
B. Account and password synchronization
C. Smartcards with PINS
D. Federated authentication
cards.why: Federated authentication lets the provider trust the company's identity provider, so users authenticate with internal credentials and the provider never stores or sees passwords.

whyNot.A: Two-factor authentication adds a factor but does not stop the provider from holding passwords.
whyNot.B: Synchronizing accounts and passwords gives the provider a copy of the credentials, violating the requirement.
whyNot.C: Smartcards with PINs replace passwords and do not meet the requirement to keep using usernames and passwords.

cards.front:
The data backup window has expanded into the morning hours and has begun to affect production users. The main bottleneck in the process is the time it takes to replicate the backups to separate severs at the offsite data center. Which of the following uses of deduplication could be implemented to reduce the backup window?
A. Implement deduplication at the network level between the two locations
B. Implement deduplication on the storage array to reduce the amount of drive space needed
C. Implement deduplication on the server storage to reduce the data backed up
D. Implement deduplication on both the local and remote servers
cards.back: B. Implement deduplication on the storage array to reduce the amount of drive space needed
cards.why: The bottleneck is replication to the offsite site, so deduplicating on the network path between locations reduces the data transferred, which is option A rather than the keyed answer.

whyNot.A: Network-level deduplication would reduce transferred data, but it is not the keyed answer.
whyNot.C: Deduplicating server storage reduces what is backed up locally but not necessarily what is replicated offsite.
whyNot.D: Deduplicating on both servers is broader but less targeted at the replication bottleneck.

cards.keyDoubt: A: Network-level deduplication between the two sites directly shrinks the replicated data, which is the stated bottleneck, whereas storage-array deduplication mainly saves disk space.

cards.front:
A penetration testing is preparing for a client engagement in which the tester must provide data that proves and validates the scanning tools' results. Which of the following is the best method for collecting this information?
A. Set up the scanning system's firewall to permit and log all outbound connections
B. Use a protocol analyzer to log all pertinent network traffic
C. Configure network flow data logging on all scanning system
D. Enable debug level logging on the scanning system and all scanning tools used.
cards.back: B. Use a protocol analyzer to log all pertinent network traffic
cards.why: A protocol analyzer captures actual packet-level traffic, providing independent evidence that proves and validates what the scanning tools reported.

whyNot.A: Permitting and logging outbound connections gives only connection metadata, not the content needed as proof.
whyNot.C: Flow data records summary conversation statistics without payload detail to validate findings.
whyNot.D: Debug logging shows the tools' own view, which is not independent validation of their results.

cards.front:
Which of the following best describes the initial processing phase used in mobile device forensics?
A. The phone should be powered down and the battery removed to preserve the state of data on any internal or removable storage utilized by the mobile device
B. The removable data storage cards should be processed first to prevent data alteration when examining the mobile device
C. The mobile device should be examined first, then removable storage and lastly the phone without removable storage should be examined again
D. The phone and storage cards should be examined as a complete unit after examining the removable storage cards separately.
cards.back: D. The phone and storage cards should be examined as a complete unit after examining the removable storage cards separately.
cards.why: The keyed answer reflects a procedure of examining removable storage separately and then the phone with its storage as a unit, though this is a loosely worded forensic sequence.

whyNot.A: Powering down and removing the battery can alter volatile data and trigger device locks.
whyNot.B: Processing storage cards first is not the standard initial step and ignores isolating the device from the network.
whyNot.C: Examining the device first risks altering data and the described sequence is illogical.

cards.front:
Ann a security analyst is monitoring the IDS console and noticed multiple connections from an internal host to a suspicious call back domain. Which of the following tools would aid her to decipher the network traffic?
A. Vulnerability Scanner
B. NMAP
C. NETSTAT
D. Packet Analyzer
cards.why: The question asks which tool deciphers network traffic, and a packet analyzer captures and decodes packet contents, so D is the better choice over the keyed NETSTAT.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses and does not decode traffic content.
whyNot.B: Nmap discovers hosts and ports and does not inspect existing traffic.
whyNot.D: A packet analyzer would decode traffic, but it is not the keyed answer.

cards.keyDoubt: D: A packet analyzer decodes the actual traffic contents, while NETSTAT only lists connections and listening ports on a host.

cards.front:
An administrator is testing the collision resistance of different hashing algorithms. Which of the following is the strongest collision resistance test?
A. Find two identical messages with different hashes
B. Find two identical messages with the same hash
C. Find a common has between two specific messages
D. Find a common hash between a specific message and a random message
cards.back: A. Find two identical messages with different hashes
cards.why: Collision resistance means it is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same hash; the keyed wording is garbled, but the strongest test is finding any such pair.

whyNot.B: Two identical messages always produce the same hash, so this is trivial and proves nothing.
whyNot.C: Finding a hash common to two specific given messages is a harder, targeted second-preimage-style task but not the standard collision definition.
whyNot.D: Matching a specific message to a random one is a preimage-style test, not general collision resistance.

cards.keyDoubt: C: Strictly, a collision means two different messages with the same hash, and none of the options states that cleanly; A as worded describes an impossible event.

cards.front:
The SSID broadcast for a wireless router has been disabled but a network administrator notices that unauthorized users are accessing the wireless network. The administer has determined that attackers are still able to detect the presence of the wireless network despite the fact the SSID has been disabled. Which of the following would further obscure the presence of the wireless network?
A. Upgrade the encryption to WPA or WPA2
B. Create a non-zero length SSID for the wireless router
C. Reroute wireless users to a honeypot
D. Disable responses to a broadcast probe request
cards.back: D. Disable responses to a broadcast probe request
cards.why: Disabling responses to broadcast probe requests stops the access point from announcing itself to active scanners, further hiding the wireless network.

whyNot.A: WPA or WPA2 strengthens encryption but does not hide the network's presence.
whyNot.B: A non-zero SSID would broadcast the network name, making it more visible.
whyNot.C: A honeypot lures attackers and does not obscure the network.

cards.front:
Which of the following should be used to implement voice encryption?
A. SSLv3
B. VDSL
C. SRTP
D. VoIP
cards.why: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) adds encryption, authentication and integrity to RTP voice and media streams.

whyNot.A: SSLv3 is a deprecated, insecure transport protocol not designed for real-time voice streams.
whyNot.B: VDSL is a broadband access technology and provides no encryption.
whyNot.D: VoIP is the voice delivery technology itself, not an encryption mechanism.

cards.front:
During an application design, the development team specifics a LDAP module for single sign-on communication with the company's access control database. This is an example of which of the following?
A. Application control
B. Data in-transit
C. Identification
D. Authentication
cards.why: LDAP in a single sign-on design verifies user credentials against a directory, which is the authentication function.

whyNot.A: Application control restricts which software can run, which is unrelated to directory lookups.
whyNot.B: Data in-transit concerns protecting data on the network, not verifying identity.
whyNot.C: Identification is claiming an identity, whereas LDAP here validates that claim.

cards.front:
After a merger, it was determined that several individuals could perform the tasks of a network administrator in the merged organization. Which of the following should have been performed to ensure that employees have proper access?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Change management
C. Periodic auditing of user credentials
D. User rights and permission review
cards.back: D. User rights and permission review
cards.why: A user rights and permission review identifies accumulated or excessive privileges, such as those resulting from merging organizations, so access matches job duties.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when access occurs, not what permissions are granted.
whyNot.B: Change management controls system changes, not user privilege assignments.
whyNot.C: Auditing credentials checks account validity and use rather than reviewing assigned rights.

cards.front:
A company exchanges information with a business partner. An annual audit of the business partner is conducted against the SLA in order to verify:
A. Performance and service delivery metrics
B. Backups are being performed and tested
C. Data ownership is being maintained and audited
D. Risk awareness is being adhered to and enforced
cards.back: A. Performance and service delivery metrics
cards.why: An SLA audit verifies that the partner meets agreed performance and service delivery metrics, such as uptime and response times.

whyNot.B: Backup testing is an operational control and is not what an SLA audit primarily verifies.
whyNot.C: Data ownership is typically defined in other agreements, not measured by SLA audits.
whyNot.D: Risk awareness enforcement is a policy matter and not an SLA metric.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the proper way to quantify the total monetary damage resulting from an exploited vulnerability?
A. Calculate the ALE
B. Calculate the ARO
C. Calculate the MTBF
D. Calculate the TCO
cards.why: Annualized Loss Expectancy (SLE multiplied by ARO) quantifies expected monetary loss from a vulnerability being exploited over a year.

whyNot.B: ARO is only the expected frequency of occurrence per year, not a monetary value.
whyNot.C: MTBF measures average time between failures and is a reliability metric.
whyNot.D: TCO is the total cost of owning an asset and does not measure exploit damage.

cards.front:
A security administrator needs to implement a system that detects possible intrusions based upon a vendor provided list. Which of the following BEST describes this type of IDS?
A. Signature based
B. Heuristic
C. Anomaly-based
D. Behavior-based
cards.why: Signature-based IDS compares activity against a vendor-supplied database of known attack patterns to detect intrusions.

whyNot.B: Heuristic detection uses rules and algorithms to spot suspicious behavior, not a fixed vendor list.
whyNot.C: Anomaly-based detection compares activity to a learned baseline rather than a predefined list.
whyNot.D: Behavior-based detection monitors for deviations in behavior and does not rely on a vendor list.

cards.front:
The chief Security Officer (CSO) has reported a rise in data loss but no break ins have occurred. By doing which of the following is the CSO most likely to reduce the number of incidents?
A. Implement protected distribution
B. Empty additional firewalls
C. Conduct security awareness training
D. Install perimeter barricades
cards.why: Data loss without break-ins points to insider or user error, so security awareness training reduces mistakes such as mishandling or leaking data.

whyNot.A: Protected distribution secures physical cabling against tapping, not accidental or insider data loss.
whyNot.B: Adding firewalls addresses external network threats, and no break-ins occurred.
whyNot.D: Perimeter barricades stop physical vehicle or intruder access, which is not the cause here.

cards.front:
Having adequate lighting on the outside of a building is an example of which of the following security controls?
A. Deterrent
B. Compensating
C. Detective
D. Preventative
cards.why: Outside lighting discourages intruders by raising the chance they are seen, which makes it a deterrent control.

whyNot.B: A compensating control substitutes for another control that cannot be implemented, which is not the case here.
whyNot.C: Detective controls identify events after or as they occur, and lighting alone does not detect anything.
whyNot.D: Preventative controls physically block access, while lighting only discourages and does not stop an intruder.

cards.front:
During a recent audit, it was discovered that several user accounts belonging to former employees were still active and had valid VPN permissions. Which of the following would help reduce the amount of risk the organization incurs in this situation in the future?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. User access reviews
C. Group-based privileges
D. Change management policies
cards.why: Regular user access reviews find and remove stale accounts, such as former employees, and verify permissions like VPN access remain appropriate.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in but do not remove orphaned accounts.
whyNot.C: Group-based privileges simplify permission assignment but do not ensure accounts are disabled after termination.
whyNot.D: Change management governs changes to systems and configurations, not user account lifecycle auditing.

cards.front:
An organization is working with a cloud services provider to transition critical business applications to a hybrid cloud environment. The organization retains sensitive customer data and wants to ensure the provider has sufficient administrative and logical controls in place to protect its data. In which of the following documents would this concern MOST likely be addressed?
A. Service level agreement
B. Interconnection security agreement
C. Non-disclosure agreement
D. Business process analysis
cards.why: A service level agreement defines the provider's contractual obligations, including security controls and performance, for the services delivered.

whyNot.B: An interconnection security agreement governs the technical connection between systems, not the provider's overall data protection controls.
whyNot.C: An NDA protects confidentiality of shared information but does not specify administrative and logical controls.
whyNot.D: A business process analysis examines internal workflows and impact, and is not an agreement with the provider.

cards.front:
A security administrator wants to implement a company-wide policy to empower data owners to manage and enforce access control rules on various resources. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Mandatory access control
B. Discretionary access control
C. Role based access control
D. Rule-based access control
cards.why: Discretionary access control lets data owners decide who can access their resources and set the access rules.

whyNot.A: Mandatory access control uses system-enforced labels set by administrators, not by data owners.
whyNot.C: Role-based access control assigns permissions by job role defined centrally, not by owner discretion.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies system-wide rules such as time or location, not owner-defined permissions.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an attack where communications between two parties are intercepted and forwarded to each party with neither party being aware of the interception and potential modification to the communications?
A. Spear phishing
B. Main-in-the-middle
C. URL hijacking
D. Transitive access
cards.why: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts and relays communications between two parties who believe they are talking directly, allowing silent modification.

whyNot.A: Spear phishing is a targeted deceptive message and does not involve intercepting live communications.
whyNot.C: URL hijacking (typosquatting) relies on mistyped domain names to redirect users, not on intercepting traffic.
whyNot.D: Transitive access is an indirect trust relationship between systems and is not an interception attack.

cards.front:
A security administrator wishes to implement a secure a method of file transfer when communicating with outside organizations. Which of the following protocols would BEST facilitate secure file transfers? (Select TWO)
A. SCP
B. TFTP
C. SNMP
D. FTP
E. SMTP
F. FTPS
cards.why: SCP runs over SSH and FTPS adds TLS to FTP, so both encrypt file transfers and credentials in transit.

whyNot.B: TFTP has no authentication or encryption, so it is insecure.
whyNot.C: SNMP is for network device management and monitoring, not file transfer.
whyNot.D: Plain FTP sends credentials and data in cleartext.
whyNot.E: SMTP is for email transport and does not securely transfer files by default.

cards.front:
A technician needs to implement a system which will properly authenticate users by their username and password only when the users are logging in from a computer in the office building. Any attempt to authenticate from a location other than the office building should be rejected. Which of the following MUST the technician implement?
A. Dual factor authentication
B. Transitive authentication
C. Single factor authentication
D. Biometric authentication
cards.why: Transitive authentication isn't the best fit; the requirement is location-based restriction, so the keyed answer is questionable, though it is the one option implying trust tied to the originating system.

whyNot.A: Dual factor authentication requires two factor types, but only username and password are specified.
whyNot.C: Single factor authentication checks the credential only and does not enforce a location restriction.
whyNot.D: Biometric authentication uses physical traits, which the scenario does not call for.

cards.keyDoubt: C: the scenario only uses username and password (a single factor), and location restriction is a contextual attribute, so none of the options is a clean fit and single factor best matches the stated credentials.

cards.front:
After correctly configuring a new wireless enabled thermostat to control the temperature of the company's meeting room, Joe, a network administrator determines that the thermostat is not connecting to the internet-based control system. Joe verifies that the thermostat received the expected network parameters and it is associated with the AP. Additionally, the other wireless mobile devices connected to the same wireless network are functioning properly. The network administrator verified that the thermostat works when tested at his residence. Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the thermostat is not connecting to the internet?
A. The company implements a captive portal
B. The thermostat is using the incorrect encryption algorithm
C. the WPA2 shared likely is incorrect
D. The company's DHCP server scope is full
cards.back: A. The company implements a captive portal
cards.why: A captive portal requires interactive web login before internet access, which a headless thermostat cannot complete even though it has an IP and association.

whyNot.B: An incorrect encryption algorithm would prevent association with the AP, but the thermostat is associated.
whyNot.C: A wrong WPA2 shared key would also prevent association, which already succeeded.
whyNot.D: A full DHCP scope would stop it receiving network parameters, but it received them.

cards.front:
A Chief Security Officer (CSO) has been unsuccessful in attempts to access the website for a potential partner (www.example.net). Which of the following rules is preventing the CSO from accessing the site? Blocked sites: *.nonews.com, *.rumorhasit.net, *.mars?
A. Rule 1: deny from inside to outside source any destination any service smtp
B. Rule 2: deny from inside to outside source any destination any service ping
C. Rule 3: deny from inside to outside source any destination {blocked sites} service http-https
D. Rule 4: deny from any to any source any destination any service any
cards.back: C. Rule 3: deny from inside to outside source any destination {blocked sites} service http-https
cards.why: The partner site is blocked by the web-filtering rule that denies HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the listed blocked sites, since the other rules do not govern web browsing to that destination.

whyNot.A: Rule 1 blocks only SMTP mail traffic, not web browsing.
whyNot.B: Rule 2 blocks only ping (ICMP), which does not affect website access.
whyNot.D: Rule 4 is a catch-all deny that would block everything, so it is not the specific reason for this one site.

cards.front:
Malware that changes its binary pattern on specific dates at specific times to avoid detection is known as a (n):
A. armored virus
B. logic bomb
C. polymorphic virus
D. Trojan
cards.why: A polymorphic virus alters its code or binary signature to evade signature-based detection.

whyNot.A: An armored virus resists analysis with obfuscation and anti-debugging, not by changing its pattern on a schedule.
whyNot.B: A logic bomb triggers a payload on a condition or date but does not change its binary pattern.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and does not inherently mutate its binary.

cards.front:
A company is planning to encrypt the files in several sensitive directories of a file server with a symmetric key. Which of the following could be used?
A. RSA
B. TwoFish
C. Diffie-Helman
D. NTLMv2
E. RIPEMD
cards.why: Twofish is a symmetric block cipher, so a single shared key can encrypt and decrypt the directory files.

whyNot.A: RSA is an asymmetric algorithm using key pairs.
whyNot.C: Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange protocol, not a file encryption cipher.
whyNot.D: NTLMv2 is an authentication protocol, not an encryption algorithm for files.
whyNot.E: RIPEMD is a hash function and does not provide reversible encryption.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a document that contains detailed information about actions that include how something will be done, when the actions will be performed, and penalties for failure?
A. MOU
B. ISA
C. BPA
D. SLA
cards.why: A service level agreement spells out how and when services are performed and the penalties for failing to meet them.

whyNot.A: An MOU expresses a general, non-binding intent between parties without detailed penalties.
whyNot.B: An ISA specifies security requirements for connecting systems, not service performance penalties.
whyNot.C: A BPA sets out the business relationship and responsibilities among partners, not detailed service timelines and penalties.

cards.front:
Which of the following are MOST susceptible to birthday attacks?
A. Hashed passwords
B. Digital certificates
C. Encryption passwords
D. One time passwords
cards.why: Birthday attacks exploit hash collisions, and hashed passwords are the item that relies on hash functions where collisions can be found.

whyNot.B: Digital certificates rely on signatures and trust chains, and are less directly targeted by birthday attacks than password hashes.
whyNot.C: Encryption passwords protect keys and are attacked by brute force or dictionary methods, not collision searches.
whyNot.D: One-time passwords are valid only briefly, so finding a collision offers little advantage.

cards.front:
Joe a computer forensic technician responds to an active compromise of a database server. Joe first collects information in memory, then collects network traffic and finally conducts an image of the hard drive. Which of the following procedures did Joe follow?
A. Order of volatility
B. Chain of custody
C. Recovery procedure
D. Incident isolation
cards.why: Collecting memory first, then network traffic, then disk follows the order of volatility, capturing the most perishable evidence first.

whyNot.B: Chain of custody documents evidence handling and transfers, not the sequence of collection.
whyNot.C: Recovery procedure restores systems to normal operation after an incident.
whyNot.D: Incident isolation contains the compromise by separating affected systems, not by ordering evidence collection.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to implement an internal communication system that will allow employees to send encrypted messages to each other. The system must also support non- repudiation. Which of the following implements all these requirements?
A. Bcrypt
B. Blowfish
C. PGP
D. SHA
cards.why: PGP uses public-key cryptography to encrypt messages and digital signatures to provide non-repudiation, so it satisfies both requirements.

whyNot.A: Bcrypt is a password hashing function and does not encrypt messages or provide non-repudiation.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric cipher that encrypts but cannot prove who sent a message.
whyNot.D: SHA is a hashing algorithm that provides integrity only, not encryption or non-repudiation.

cards.front:
Given the log output: Max 15 00:15:23.431 CRT: #SEC_LOGIN-5-LOGIN_SUCCESS: Login Success [user: msmith] [Source: 10.0.12.45] [localport: 23] at 00:15:23:431 CET Sun Mar 15 2015 Which of the following should the network administrator do to protect data security?
A. Configure port security for logons
B. Disable telnet and enable SSH
C. Configure an AAA server
D. Disable password and enable RSA authentication
cards.back: B. Disable telnet and enable SSH
cards.why: The log shows a successful login on port 23, which is Telnet and sends credentials and data in cleartext. Replacing it with SSH encrypts the session.

whyNot.A: Port security restricts switch ports by MAC address and does not encrypt Telnet traffic.
whyNot.C: An AAA server centralizes authentication and accounting but the Telnet session would still be unencrypted.
whyNot.D: Disabling passwords for RSA authentication does not fix cleartext transport over Telnet.

cards.front:
The firewall administrator is adding a new certificate for the company's remote access solution. The solution requires that the uploaded file contain the entire certificate chain for the certificate to load properly. The administrator loads the company certificate and the root CA certificate into the file. The file upload is rejected. Which of the following is required to complete the certificate chain?
A. Certificate revocation list
B. Intermediate authority
C. Recovery agent
D. Root of trust
cards.why: A complete chain runs from the end-entity certificate through any intermediate CA to the root CA. The missing piece is the intermediate authority certificate.

whyNot.A: A CRL lists revoked certificates and is not part of the certificate chain.
whyNot.C: A recovery agent can recover encrypted data keys and has no role in a certificate chain.
whyNot.D: The root of trust is the root CA, which the administrator already included in the file.

cards.front:
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a major defense contracting company a traveling overseas for a conference. The CEO will be taking a laptop. Which of the following should the security administrator implement to ensure confidentiality of the data if the laptop were to be stolen or lost during the trip?
A. Remote wipe
B. Full device encryption
C. BIOS password
D. GPS tracking
cards.why: Full device encryption protects data at rest so a stolen or lost laptop's contents remain unreadable without the key, preserving confidentiality.

whyNot.A: Remote wipe needs network connectivity and can be blocked, so it does not reliably protect data.
whyNot.C: A BIOS password does not encrypt data, and the drive can be removed and read elsewhere.
whyNot.D: GPS tracking helps locate the device but does nothing to protect the data on it.

cards.front:
In an effort to reduce data storage requirements, some company devices to hash every file and eliminate duplicates. The data processing routines are time sensitive so the hashing algorithm is fast and supported on a wide range of systems. Which of the following algorithms is BEST suited for this purpose?
A. MD5
B. SHA
C. RIPEMD
D. AES
cards.why: SHA family hashes are fast, widely supported, and collision resistant enough to identify duplicate files reliably for deduplication.

whyNot.A: MD5 is fast and widely supported but has known collision weaknesses, so it is a poorer choice for reliably identifying duplicates.
whyNot.C: RIPEMD is a hash but has far less support across systems than SHA.
whyNot.D: AES is a symmetric encryption algorithm, not a hashing algorithm.

cards.keyDoubt: A. MD5 is fast and universally supported, and CompTIA-era dedup questions often key it, though SHA is the more defensible modern answer.

cards.front:
A new security policy in an organization requires that all file transfers within the organization be completed using applications that provide secure transfer. Currently, the organization uses FTP and HTTP to transfer files. Which of the following should the organization implement in order to be compliant with the new policy?
A. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with TLS
B. Replace FTP with FTPS and replaces HTTP with TFTP
C. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with Telnet
D. Replace FTP with FTPS and replaces HTTP with IPSec
cards.back: A. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with TLS
cards.why: SFTP secures file transfer in place of FTP, and TLS (HTTPS) secures web traffic in place of HTTP, so both protocols are replaced with encrypted equivalents.

whyNot.B: TFTP is an insecure protocol with no encryption or authentication, so it does not replace HTTP securely.
whyNot.C: Telnet is a cleartext remote access protocol and is not a secure file transfer method.
whyNot.D: IPSec is a network layer tunnel suite, not an application that replaces HTTP for file transfer.

cards.front:
A product manager is concerned about continuing operations at a facility located in a region undergoing significant political unrest. After consulting with senior management, a decision is made to suspend operations at the facility until the situation stabilizes. Which of the following risk management strategies BEST describes management's response?
A. Deterrence
B. Mitigation
C. Avoidance
D. Acceptance
cards.why: Avoidance means eliminating the risk by stopping the risky activity entirely, which is what suspending operations at the facility does.

whyNot.A: Deterrence discourages threat actors from acting and does not remove the activity.
whyNot.B: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact while the activity continues, but operations here are halted.
whyNot.D: Acceptance means tolerating the risk and continuing operations, the opposite of suspending them.

cards.front:
Joe notices there are several user accounts on the local network generating spam with embedded malicious code. Which of the following technical control should Joe put in place to BEST reduce these incidents?
A. Account lockout
B. Group Based Privileges
C. Least privilege
D. Password complexity
cards.why: Account lockout limits repeated failed attempts, which hinders attackers from brute forcing the accounts used to send spam with malicious code.

whyNot.B: Group based privileges simplify permission assignment and do not stop compromised accounts from sending spam.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits what an account can access but does not stop it from sending email.
whyNot.D: Password complexity makes guessing harder but is a weaker control than lockout against ongoing abuse.

cards.keyDoubt: C. Least privilege is the more general control for limiting what compromised accounts can do, though the key of A is a commonly published answer.

cards.front:
Two users need to securely share encrypted files via email. Company policy prohibits users from sharing credentials or exchanging encryption keys. Which of the following can be implemented to enable users to share encrypted data while abiding by company policies?
A. Key escrow
B. Digital signatures
C. PKI
D. Hashing
cards.why: PKI lets each user encrypt with the recipient's public key and decrypt with their own private key, so no credentials or keys need to be exchanged.

whyNot.A: Key escrow stores keys with a third party for recovery and does not enable secure sharing between users.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures prove origin and integrity but do not encrypt the files.
whyNot.D: Hashing is one way and cannot encrypt files for recipients to read.

cards.front:
An information system owner has supplied a new requirement to the development team that calls for increased non-repudiation within the application. After undergoing several audits, the owner determined that current levels of non-repudiation were insufficient. Which of the following capabilities would be MOST appropriate to consider implementing is response to the new requirement?
A. Transitive trust
B. Symmetric encryption
C. Two-factor authentication
D. Digital signatures
E. One-time passwords
cards.why: Digital signatures bind a message or action to the signer's private key, providing non-repudiation because the signer cannot credibly deny it.

whyNot.A: Transitive trust extends trust between entities and does not prove who performed an action.
whyNot.B: Symmetric encryption uses a shared key, so either party could have created the data.
whyNot.C: Two-factor authentication strengthens login but does not provide proof of origin for transactions.
whyNot.E: One-time passwords authenticate a session but do not create a verifiable signature to prevent denial.

cards.front:
Joe a website administrator believes he owns the intellectual property for a company invention and has been replacing image files on the company's public facing website in the DMZ. Joe is using steganography to hide stolen data. Which of the following controls can be implemented to mitigate this type of inside threat?
A. Digital signatures
B. File integrity monitoring
C. Access controls
D. Change management
E. Stateful inspection firewall
cards.why: File integrity monitoring detects unauthorized changes to files such as replaced images by comparing hashes against a known baseline.

whyNot.A: Digital signatures on images would not stop an authorized admin from replacing files or detect steganography by themselves.
whyNot.C: Access controls are already in place, since Joe is an administrator with legitimate write access.
whyNot.D: Change management is a process control that Joe could bypass and does not technically detect modifications.
whyNot.E: A stateful firewall filters network traffic and cannot detect file changes made by an insider.

cards.front:
The process of applying a salt and cryptographic hash to a password then repeating the process many times is known as which of the following?
A. Collision resistance
B. Rainbow table
C. Key stretching
D. Brute force attack
cards.why: Key stretching, as in PBKDF2 or bcrypt, repeatedly hashes a salted password to make brute force attacks computationally expensive.

whyNot.A: Collision resistance describes a hash property that makes two inputs producing the same output hard to find.
whyNot.B: A rainbow table is a precomputed hash lookup attack, not a defensive process.
whyNot.D: A brute force attack is the attack that key stretching is meant to slow down.

cards.front:
Which of the following is commonly used for federated identity management across multiple organizations?
A. SAML
B. Active Directory
C. Kerberos
D. LDAP
cards.why: SAML exchanges authentication and authorization assertions between identity providers and service providers across organizations, enabling federated single sign-on.

whyNot.B: Active Directory manages identities within a single organization's domain or forest.
whyNot.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based protocol used mainly within one realm or domain.
whyNot.D: LDAP is a directory access protocol and does not itself provide cross-organization federation.

cards.front:
While performing surveillance activities, an attacker determines that an organization is using 802.1X to secure LAN access. Which of the following attack mechanisms can the attacker utilize to bypass the identified network security?
A. MAC spoofing
B. Pharming
C. Xmas attack
D. ARP poisoning
cards.why: 802.1X often permits devices by MAC address or leaves printers and phones on MAC bypass, so an attacker can spoof an authorized device's MAC address.

whyNot.B: Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS manipulation and does not bypass port-based network access control.
whyNot.C: An Xmas attack is a port scan using unusual TCP flags and does not defeat 802.1X.
whyNot.D: ARP poisoning redirects traffic on a network the attacker has already joined, so it does not bypass 802.1X.

cards.front:
A security administrator has been asked to implement a VPN that will support remote access over IPSEC. Which of the following is an encryption algorithm that would meet this requirement?
A. MD5
B. AES
C. UDP
D. PKI
cards.why: AES is a symmetric encryption algorithm supported by IPSec for encrypting the ESP payload in VPN tunnels.

whyNot.A: MD5 is a hashing algorithm, not an encryption algorithm.
whyNot.C: UDP is a transport layer protocol and does not encrypt data.
whyNot.D: PKI is a trust framework for managing certificates and keys, not an encryption algorithm.

cards.front:
A security administrator is evaluating three different services: radius, diameter, and Kerberos. Which of the following is a feature that is UNIQUE to Kerberos?
A. It provides authentication services
B. It uses tickets to identify authenticated users
C. It provides single sign-on capability
D. It uses XML for cross-platform interoperability
cards.back: B. It uses tickets to identify authenticated users
cards.why: Kerberos uses tickets issued by a Key Distribution Center to prove identity, which is the mechanism unique to it compared with RADIUS and Diameter.

whyNot.A: RADIUS and Diameter also provide authentication services, so this is not unique.
whyNot.C: Single sign-on is not exclusive to Kerberos; other federated systems offer it too.
whyNot.D: Kerberos does not use XML; XML-based interoperability relates to SAML, not Kerberos.

cards.front:
Which of the following can affect electrostatic discharge in a network operations center?
A. Fire suppression
B. Environmental monitoring
C. Proximity card access
D. Humidity controls
cards.why: Low humidity allows static charge to build up, so humidity controls directly influence electrostatic discharge risk to equipment in a NOC.

whyNot.A: Fire suppression deals with extinguishing fires and does not affect static buildup.
whyNot.B: Environmental monitoring only observes conditions and does not itself change ESD risk.
whyNot.C: Proximity card access controls physical entry and has no effect on electrostatic discharge.

cards.front:
A malicious attacker has intercepted HTTP traffic and inserted an ASCII line that sets the referrer URL. Which of the following is the attacker most likely utilizing?
A. Header manipulation
B. Cookie hijacking
C. Cross-site scripting
D. Xml injection
cards.why: Inserting a line that sets the referrer into intercepted HTTP traffic is header manipulation, where the attacker alters HTTP header fields.

whyNot.B: Cookie hijacking steals or reuses session cookies rather than altering the referrer header.
whyNot.C: Cross-site scripting injects script into web pages, not a header line into traffic.
whyNot.D: XML injection targets XML parsers and data, not HTTP headers.

cards.front:
A company would like to prevent the use of a known set of applications from being used on company computers. Which of the following should the security administrator implement?
A. Whitelisting
B. Anti-malware
C. Application hardening
D. Blacklisting
E. Disable removable media
cards.why: Blacklisting blocks a known set of unwanted applications while allowing everything else to run.

whyNot.A: Whitelisting allows only approved applications, which is stricter than blocking a known set.
whyNot.B: Anti-malware detects malicious code and does not enforce a list of prohibited applications.
whyNot.C: Application hardening secures an application's configuration and does not block specific programs.
whyNot.E: Disabling removable media limits one delivery path but does not prevent the listed applications from running.

cards.front:
A new hire wants to use a personally owned phone to access company resources. The new hire expresses concern about what happens to the data on the phone when they leave the company. Which of the following portions of the company's mobile device management configuration would allow the company data to be removed from the device without touching the new hire's data?
A. Asset control
B. Device access control
C. Storage lock out
D. Storage segmentation
cards.why: Storage segmentation separates corporate data from personal data on a BYOD device, so the company can remove its data without touching personal data.

whyNot.A: Asset control tracks and inventories devices and does not separate data containers.
whyNot.B: Device access control restricts who can use the device or resources, not data separation.
whyNot.C: Storage lock out locks the device after failed attempts and does not partition data.

cards.front:
A consultant has been tasked to assess a client's network. The client reports frequent network outages. Upon viewing the spanning tree configuration, the consultant notices that an old and law performing edge switch on the network has been elected to be the root bridge. Which of the following explains this scenario?
A. The switch also serves as the DHCP server
B. The switch has the lowest MAC address
C. The switch has spanning tree loop protection enabled
D. The switch has the fastest uplink port
cards.back: B. The switch has the lowest MAC address
cards.why: Spanning tree elects the root bridge by lowest bridge ID, and with equal priorities the lowest MAC address wins, even on an old slow switch.

whyNot.A: Serving as a DHCP server has no bearing on root bridge election.
whyNot.C: Loop protection prevents unexpected root changes and does not cause a switch to be elected root.
whyNot.D: Uplink speed affects path cost, not which switch is elected root bridge.

cards.front:
An organization is trying to decide which type of access control is most appropriate for the network. The current access control approach is too complex and requires significant overhead. Management would like to simplify the access control and provide user with the ability to determine what permissions should be applied to files, document, and directories. The access control method that BEST satisfies these objectives is:
A. Rule-based access control
B. Role-based access control
C. Mandatory access control
D. Discretionary access control
